title: Who were the top teen athletes at the Asian Games?
body: Who were the top teen athletes at the Asian Games? | Athletics | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up EXPLAINER Sport | Athletics Who were the top teen athletes at the Asian Games? China’s Zhang Zhanshuo, 19, finished with seven gold medals while compatriot Yu Zidi won three record-breaking golds. Listen Listen (7 mins) Save Share Who were the top teen athletes at the Asian Games? on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Shin Ohashi of Japan poses on the podium after the men's 200m breaststroke final [Atsushi Tomura/Getty Images] By Anushe Engineer and Reuters Published On 5 Oct 2026 5 Oct 2026 Teenage athletes have headlined some of the biggest Asian Games triumphs, leading their countries to historic gold medals, breaking records and cementing their legacy as formidable forces in the field. Far from being intimidated by competitors double or triple their age, these schoolchildren remained cool and unfazed as they cruised to gold at their Asian Games debut. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 How a comedy of errors ‘ruined everything’ for athletes at the Asian Games list 2 of 4 China swimmer makes Asian Games history as Thai sprinter wins track 100m list 3 of 4 Malaysia’s Ng, Sivasangari book 2028 Olympics berth with Asian Games gold list 4 of 4 Asian Games: Rumesh Pathirage wins javelin gold, Arshad Nadeem is fourth end of list Many are already familiar with the pressure and expectations of the world stage and have dominated their sport all season. Al Jazeera Sport looks at some of the stars who left their mark in Japan: Yu Zidi, 13 China: Swimming At just 13, Yu was named female Most Valuable Player (MVP), as she bagged three gold medals and broke as many Asian Games records in a fairytale debut. The schoolgirl stormed to victory in the women’s 200m butterfly, 200m and 400m individual medley (IM) and had a comfortable lead over her competitors. Her time of two minutes and 6.10 seconds (2:06.10) in the 200m IM stands as a world junior record and second-fastest time ever. “I don’t think I am what people describe as a prodigy,” she said after being crowned MVP. “I will continue to train hard, push myself and work alongside young athletes across Asia to inspire more young people to love and take part in sports, especially swimming.” Yu Zidi celebrates after winning the 400m Individual Medley [Atsushi Tomura/Getty Images] Zhang Zhanshuo, 19 China: Swimming Zhang held up seven fingers after his 400m freestyle win to count out his gold medals at the Games – the most at this edition, and more than what 27 of the 45 participating nations had in their medal tally at the conclusion of the event. Advertisement He set Games records in the 400m and 800m freestyle, an Asian record in the 200m, and helped power China to gold and Asian records in the men’s 4x100m and 4x200m freestyle relays. But the 19-year-old has bigger victories in sight. “The Asian Games is not the goal. I’m still aiming for the Olympics and competing with the best,” he said. The teenager’s haul helped China sign off from swimming with 30 golds out of 41 medal events in the pool, with chief rival Japan a distant second with seven titles. Zhang at the end of the men’s 400m freestyle [Andy Chua/Reuters] Shin Ohashi, 17 Japan: Swimming Ohashi broke the world record in the men’s 200m breaststroke (2:04.83) in front of a home crowd to become the first swimmer under the 2:05 mark. The gold added to his title in the 100m breaststroke shared with China’s Dong Zhihao, bronze in the 50m breaststroke, and silver in the mixed and men’s 4x100m medley relays. The teenager said he was surprised and honoured that Olympic champion Leon Marchand knew who he was, after the Frenchman described the 17-year-old as a “scary” prospect ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. “I respect him because I know just how strong he is. But if I want to win, he’s someone I know I’ll have to beat.” Ohashi’s world record performance came just a week after the teenager recovered from COVID-19. Shin Ohashi broke the world record in men’s 200m breaststroke [Atsushi Tomura/Getty Images] Yan Ziyi, 18 China: Athletics Yan was already javelin world number one and Asian record holder when she stepped onto the field for her Games debut – her first and only throw of 70.46 metres was enough for gold and a Games record. It was the sixth-best of all time and well ahead of Olympic champion and home hero Haruka Kitaguchi’s 62.70m. Yan is closing in on the world record of 72.28m set by Barbora Spotakova in 2008. In May, she hurled a world-leading, record-breaking 71.74m to open an unprecedented season. Yan during the women’s javelin throw final [Mohd Rasfan/AFP] Chen Yujie, 17 China: Athletics Chen stormed to a new Games record in the women’s 100m en route to her first gold as she announced herself as the new sprint queen in Asia. “I have no limits,” was her response when asked how much faster she hopes to run. She followed up her podium finish with a silver in the 200m and gold in the women’s and mixed 4x100m relays. Chen celebrates after winning the women’s 100m final [Mohd Rasfan/AFP] Taiju Goto, 17 Japan: Athletics Goto narrowly missed gold in the men’s 400m hurdles, but his 47.93s was enough for a world under-18 best time, Asian under-20 best time, and a new personal best. Advertisement The teen star has run sub-50 seconds eight times this season alone, an impressive feat for a 17-year-old. His Asian Games silver added to the World Under-20 one he bagged in August. Bassem Hemeida of Qatar crosses the finish line to win the gold medal ahead of Japan’s Taiju Goto in the men’s 400m hurdles final [Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images] Kumkum Mohod, 17 India: Archery Mohod scripted history for India when she became the first Indian to win an individual recurve archery gold at the Games. The 17-year-old helped India to gold in the women’s team recurve, and partnered with Dhiraj Bommadevara for mixed team silver. Mohod’s gold was no stroke of luck; she defeated South Korea’s reigning world champion and Olympic medallist Kang Chaeyoung in the quarterfinals before dominating China’s Zhu Jingyi in the semifinals. “Ever since I’ve made it to the national team, I’ve been visualising this moment. I had visualised shooting an X, and that is exactly what happened,” she told reporters after the match, according to Indian media. Kumkum Anil Mohod [Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters] Anahat Singh, 18 India: Squash World junior champion Anahat Singh has been India’s finest in the sport for several years now. Despite only being 18, Aichi-Nagoya was Singh’s second Asian Games outing after competing at Hangzhou 2023, where she won two bronze medals in the mixed doubles and women’s team events. This time round, she won a silver in the women’s singles against world number five Sivasangari Subramaniam of Malaysia. However, her semifinal match against Japan’s Satomi Watanabe was what she called the “best win” of her career after producing a stellar comeback to defeat the world number six. India’s Anahat Singh in action during the women’s singles gold medal match [Chalinee Thirasupa/Reuters] Yuki Kurihara, 11 Japan: e-sports At just 11 years of age, e-sports prodigy Kurihara became the youngest gold medallist in Asian Games history when he won Puyo Puyo Champions. “I’m really happy. The gold medal is really beautiful, shiny and heavy,” Kurihara said after his final, where he barely broke a sweat. Kurihara started playing Puyo Puyo in his first year of primary school – where he still studies – and soon started competing and winning in tournaments. He obtained his pro licence in April this year and regularly beats adults, often triple his age. Yuki Kurihara of Japan poses on the podium [Toru Hanai/Getty Images] Ku Yong-yan, 12 Taipei: Skateboarding Ku took silver in the men’s skateboarding park with 87.33 points, and was just one of several teenagers – in his case, a pre-teen – who medalled in skateboarding at the Games. Japan’s Izuru Nagahara, 15, took gold in the event. China’s Zhu Yuanling, also 15, won gold in the women’s street skateboarding competition. China’s Cao Shiqi finished fourth in women’s skateboarding park and was the youngest athlete in China’s delegation at the Games. title: The 2029 tipping point: Western populations are about to start shrinking, piling pressure on public finances
body:
2029 tipping point: Aging Western populations set to strain public finances Skip Navigation Markets Pre-Markets U.S. Markets Currencies Prediction Markets Cryptocurrency Futures & Commodities Bonds Funds & ETFs Business Economy Finance Health & Science Media Real Estate Energy Climate Transportation Investigations Industrials Retail Wealth Sports Life Small Business Investing Personal Finance Fintech Financial Advisors Options Action ETF Street Buffett Archive Earnings Trader Talk Tech Cybersecurity AI Enterprise Internet Media Mobile Social Media CNBC Disruptor 50 Tech Guide Politics & Policy White House Policy Defense Congress Expanding Opportunity Video Latest Video Full Episodes Livestream Live Audio Live TV Schedule CNBC Podcasts CEO Interviews CNBC Documentaries Digital Originals Watchlist Investing Club Trust Portfolio Analysis Trade Alerts Meeting Videos Homestretch Jim's Columns Education Subscribe PRO Pro News Josh Brown Mike Santoli Calls of the Day My Portfolio Livestream Full Episodes Stock Screener Market Forecast Options Investing Chart Investing Subscribe Livestream Menu Make It select USA INTL Livestream Search quotes, news & videos Livestream Watchlist SIGN IN Create free account Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Economy The 2029 tipping point: Western populations are about to start shrinking, piling pressure on public finances Published Mon, Oct 5 2026 1:00 AM EDT Elsa Ohlen WATCH LIVE Key Points Europe's population will peak in 2029 according to forecasts, while the U.S.'s lies further ahead but is heavily dependent on immigration. Moody's says the fiscal pressures from aging emerge long before populations actually start shrinking. AI and increased productivity can only partially offset the long-term challenge of an aging workforce, Chemla said. watch now VIDEO 4:12 04:12 Moody's: AI will not soften population drag on growth Squawk Box Europe As Western populations age, fewer workers and higher costs will strain public finances, credit rating agency Moody's has warned. Europe is at the sharp end of the demographic shift. The European Union's population is projected to peak as soon as 2029, "after which a sustained long-term decline will begin," according to the European Commission. The U.S. Census Bureau does not expect the American population to peak until 2080 under its main projection , or until 2043 under its low-immigration scenario. Excluding immigration impact, the population decline has already started. But Moody's says the fiscal pressures from aging emerge long before populations actually start shrinking. Today, G7 economies have about three working-age people for every person over 65. That ratio is expected to fall to around two by 2050, putting further pressure on growth and public finances, including healthcare systems, according to Moody's. Aging populations affect economies through slower economic growth, greater pressure on public finances from pension and care costs, changing consumer demand, and shifts in real interest rates and sovereign yields, Olivier Chemla, vice president of credit strategy and standards at Moody's, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday. watch now VIDEO 4:12 04:12 Moody's: AI will not soften population drag on growth Squawk Box Europe In a report published last week, Moody's forecasts that the world's aging populations will have fundamental impacts on the global economy and lead to difficult policy decisions. While population growth has long been a tailwind for growth and creditworthiness, falling fertility rates and unprecedented speed of changing age structures are now changing that picture, Moody's writes. "Fewer workers will limit productive capacity, while fewer households and consumers will weaken demand. As a result, countries will have to rely more on productivity to sustain growth," the report states. The AI impact AI and increased productivity can only partially offset the long-term challenge of an aging workforce, Chemla said. "This is a partial mitigant because you can certainly replace and enhance the supply side of the economy in factories and in services, but at the same time, robots do not consume – at least not yet – and so on the demand side, you will still be having that gap, which will slow growth," he added. And it's not only Europe and the U.S., but emerging economies are aging rapidly, too. China's share of people aged 65 and over has doubled from 7% to 14% over the past two decades, with Brazil, Thailand and Turkiye on similar trajectories. These countries will face the costs of aging at much lower income levels than the advanced economies that aged before them, the report says, noting that in Europe, the same shift took several decades. title: France closes up to 500 schools Monday over student protests
body: Up to 500 schools close in France over student protests - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East France closes up to 500 schools Monday over student protests Image source, Reuters Image caption, French riot police were deployed to the manage the protests on Friday By Jack Burgess Published 4 October 2026 Updated 2 hours ago Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday. Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Édouard Geffray said. He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests. Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille. High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. On Friday, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests. The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons". "There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Édouard Geffray claimed. "Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before". On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Over 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according the AFP news agency, with around 85% of them minors. Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France Published 2 days ago School protests send shivers down French government's spine Published 2 days ago Organisers of the protests have called for the demonstrations to continue on Tuesday after accusing the government of a lack of "concrete measures", according to AFP. On Sunday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his government is taking further steps to "address the difficulties faced by high school students and educational staff". He said this includes ensuring classes continue, improving facilities, better organising school days and making the French university admissions platform more transparent. Lecornu also said the government is accelerating the review of its "vandal-pays" bill to ensure that people responsible for damage bear the cost of their actions. title: All six passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
body: All passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East All six passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast Image source, Reuters Image caption, Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard the flight, which went missing in the early hours of Saturday By Gavin Butler Published 5 October 2026, 04:33 BST Updated 3 hours ago Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator. On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island. "We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter. "Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues." The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning. On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft. The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT). Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard. "This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening. "Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day." Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home. Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News. FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft). Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net. "You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?" The pilot's response was inaudible. "You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe. The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency. An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue". The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar". Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations. "Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said. title: Nearly 1,500 migrants arrive in Myanmar from Malaysia despite UN warnings
body: Nearly 1,500 migrants arrive in Myanmar from Malaysia despite UN warnings | Refugees News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Refugees Nearly 1,500 migrants arrive in Myanmar from Malaysia despite UN warnings Malaysia continues mass refugee deportations despite warnings from the UN about unsafe conditions in an active war zone. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share Nearly 1,500 migrants arrive in Myanmar from Malaysia despite UN warnings on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info A bus carrying Myanmar nationals being repatriated from Malaysia to the war-torn country heads towards the naval base in Lumut, on the outskirts of Kuala Lumpur, on September 29, 2026 [AFP] By AFP and AP Published On 5 Oct 2026 5 Oct 2026 Nearly 1,500 Myanmar refugees and migrants deported from Malaysia have arrived in their war-ravaged country under an opaque repatriation scheme heavily criticised by human rights groups and the United Nations refugee agency. The 1,479 returnees, transported from Malaysia on board two navy warships and a hospital ship on Tuesday, arrived in southern Yangon early Sunday, Nay Lin Tun, a regional government minister, said. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Malaysia gave refuge to Rohingya; now it wants them to go list 2 of 3 Malaysia sends Rohingya back to Myanmar despite safety warnings list 3 of 3 ‘They are crying’: Refugees in Malaysia in fear amid Myanmar deportation end of list They are among 5,000 Myanmar nationals who will be repatriated in stages from Malaysia, where more than 10,300 others are being held in immigration detention centres, according to the country’s Home Ministry. Malaysia insists all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation, but rights monitors have raised concerns that Myanmar refugees had little choice and warned that conditions for return remain unsafe. The UN refugee agency said this past week that its staff were not allowed to meet the Myanmar nationals to confirm whether their decisions to return “were genuinely free and informed”. Rohingya make up the majority of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, but it remains unclear how many members of the persecuted Rohingya are among the returned group. The deportation was carried out during escalating raids on refugee communities in Malaysia by immigration officials, which led to the detention of more than 50,000 refugees in 2026. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced the repatriations in July against a backdrop of rising xenophobia towards refugees, particularly the Rohingya. Advertisement Kuala Lumpur is moving ahead with plans to return a second group of more than 3,500 refugees and migrants, saying they have caused financial, social and security burdens. While Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants, it is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). This includes more than 126,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya refugees. Myanmar pledged last month that returns will be “safe and dignified”. But Yap Lay Sheng, a senior human rights specialist with Fortify Rights, told the AFP news agency: “There’s no telling how the regime would treat returnees.” Myanmar has been accused of committing genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority. Earlier this year, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) opened its first genocide case it has heard in full in more than a decade. The UNHCR and rights groups said returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone. Myanmar has been embroiled in a civil war since the military seized power from the elected government in 2021. The war has killed more than 100,000 people since the coup, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project. Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing, the military coup leader who was installed as civilian president in April, is expected to visit Malaysia soon to discuss the repatriation scheme. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network

title: Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff
body: Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Brazil Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff Dmytro Hubenko | Wesley Rahn with Reuters, AFP, AP Published 10/04/2026 Published October 4, 2026 last updated 10/05/2026 last updated October 5, 2026 Populist Flavio Bolsonaro has secured a thin lead over incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but the next president of Brazil will be decided in the runoff round, according to the country’s electoral court. https://p.dw.com/p/5NiO9 The early count in the Brazilian presidential election puts Flavio Bolsonaro (left) ahead of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva Image: Alexandre Meneghini/Pilar Olivares/REUTERS Advertisement With votes being counted in Brazil following the presidential election on Sunday, populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro was leading the race ahead of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro seeks to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro, while Lula is seeking his fourth non-consecutive term. Commenting on the outcome, Lula said they were "unexpected" as he was convinced he would "win in the first round." "We are in extra time," the 80-year-old said. "In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people." With more than 99% of the ballots processed, Flavio Bolsonaro has received 47.2% of the vote. Lula has 45%, according to the electoral court. Since neither candidate received enough votes to win outright on Sunday, the court announced that Bolsonaro and Lula will face each other in a runoff. Bolsonaro is monitoring the vote count in Brasilia, the country's capital, while Lula is following it from Sao Paulo. Because Brazil uses electronic voting machines, final results are expected to be available within several hours of the polls closing. You can watch our livestream on the Brazil election results below. Right gaining momentum in Brazil Fabio de Sa e Silva, a professor of Brazilian studies at the University of Oklahoma, told DW that the right was currently on the rise in Brazil, making it difficult for Lula to change the course of the election. "He still has a chance, based on the numbers, but the momentum is with the right," said de Sa e Silva. "The big news tomorrow will be not that we have a runoff... but it is a takeover that happened in Congress by the far-right," the researcher said. He added that it will be very hard for Lula to govern with Brazil's new Congress, even if he eventually secures another term. Lula vows to 'defeat the far right' Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo. Long queues of voters were seen in parts of Rio de Janeiro Image: Bruna Prado/AP Photo/picture alliance The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right ." Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city. Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution. "The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday. The 80-year-old Lula is seeking the presidency for a fourth and final time Image: Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS Bolsonaro calls for 'change' Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana. He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him. Flavio Bolsonaro has said he would pardon his father if elected Image: Douglas Shineidr/AFP The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent." "Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed." Brazil's 2022 election rematch The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected. Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump , who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial.  The US president called the case a "witch hunt." Brazilians vote in high-stakes presidential election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference." Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change. Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely." US President Trump had held close ties with fellow right-wing populist Jair Bolsonaro [FILE March 2019] Image: Chris Kleponis/CNP/MediaPunch/picture alliance What happens next? Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media. In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct. Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency. In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%. In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points. Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators. body: Israel face spitting allegation as Ireland boss ‘delighted’ games are over | Football | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Navigation menu caret-left Israel-Palestine conflict Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons ‘This is an apartheid regime’ Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? History of flotilla campaigns caret-right Sport | Football Israel face spitting allegation as Ireland boss ‘delighted’ games are over Ireland manager says ‘disciplinary committee will look at’ allegations that Israeli player spat at one of his coaching staff. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share Israel face spitting allegation as Ireland boss ‘delighted’ games are over on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Players and officials tussle as the teams leave the pitch at half-time in the UEFA Nations League B match between the Republic of Ireland and Israel [Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile via Getty Images] By Reuters Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 Tempers flared ‌again as Ireland and Israel drew 1-1 on Sunday in the second of their two UEFA Nations ⁠League meetings, concluding a fortnight ⁠dominated as much by political tensions as football. Ireland had faced calls from some supporters and politicians to boycott the fixtures before beating Israel 3-0 behind closed doors in Hungary in their first meeting ⁠a week ago. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 ‘Everyone knew’: Canada boss Marsch wants Man City relegated for breaches list 2 of 4 Cristiano Ronaldo can return to Portugal team if he wants, says Jesus list 3 of 4 Amid teen triumph and organisational chaos, Asian Games close in Japan list 4 of 4 FC Barcelona accused of corruption in Negreira case: All you need to know end of list “I’m absolutely delighted this is finished,” Ireland’s Icelandic coach Heimir Hallgrimsson told reporters. “It’s taken a toll out of us all. I’ve given so much credit to the players. They have been absolutely amazing in tough times, and I ⁠wish no national team to go through what we have gone through for the last two weeks.” Ireland is one of Europe’s most outspoken critics of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and the Football Association of Ireland chose to stage Sunday’s match behind closed doors in Serbia amid the pressure to withdraw from the fixtures. The absence of supporters, however, did little to ease the tension on ‌the pitch. Irish media reported that one of Ireland’s coaches, Damien Doyle, had accused an Israeli player of spitting at him after the half-time whistle. Asked about the spitting incident at the post-match news conference, Hallgrimsson declined to provide details. “I was there. I’m not going to comment. It’s something a disciplinary committee will look at,” he told reporters. Israel coach Ran Ben-Shimon said he had already left the sideline and did not see what happened. “Halftime, I was in the dressing room, in my room with my ⁠staff; I didn’t see anything. When I’m going to see and check, I will get ⁠back to you with the answer,” he told reporters. Advertisement Tense Ireland-Israel atmosphere again in Nations League As in the first meeting, there were no pre-match handshakes or exchange of pennants, while players from each team bowed their heads during the opposing national anthem. Ireland again wore black armbands commemorating the victims of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, ⁠with the Israelis sporting black armbands in memory of the victims of the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel that sparked the war. Troy Parrott gave Ireland the lead with a 39th-minute penalty, ⁠but Dor Peretz levelled immediately after the break for Israel with their first ⁠effort on target. Israel hit the woodwork twice in the second half of a poor game in which neither side could fashion a winner. The draw left Ireland third in Group B3 on five points, three behind leaders Austria, with second-placed Kosovo ahead of them on goal difference. Israel are at the bottom with ‌two points. Ben-Shimon welcomed his team’s response to the 3-0 defeat and rejected suggestions his players had been overly aggressive. “When I come to a game, I say to my players, ‘This is the best way to play the cleanest football as ‌you ‌can, but be aggressive’, OK? I never say to injure someone; this is not our way. title: Manchester City must be relegated, says Canada’s ex-Leeds manager
body: Manchester City charges: ‘Everyone knew’ – Marsch says relegation to follow | Football | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Sport | Football Manchester City charges: ‘Everyone knew’ – Marsch says relegation to follow Jesse Marsch alleges Man City’s financial wrongdoing was widely known in the Premier League, and relegation must follow. Listen Listen (2 mins) Save Share ‘Everyone knew’: Canada boss Marsch wants Man City relegated for breaches on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Jesse Marsch reacts during his time as Leeds United manager as then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola looks on [Phil Noble/Reuters] By Reuters Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 Canada coach Jesse Marsch has ‌called for Manchester City to be punished severely over breaches of Premier League ⁠financial rules, saying his ⁠experience managing against the club left him convinced there were inconsistencies in the way it operated. City were found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League’s ⁠financial rules over nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, with the league alleging the club used “sham” commercial contracts to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.19bn). Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 FC Barcelona accused of corruption in Negreira case: All you need to know list 2 of 3 Amid teen triumph and organisational chaos, Asian Games close in Japan list 3 of 3 Ireland refuse handshake with Israel and don armbands in Nations League tie end of list The club has denied wrongdoing, saying the verdict contained material errors of law, principle and fact, and filed an appeal on Thursday against the independent commission’s ruling. Marsch, who managed Leeds United from 2022 to 2023, said the disparity between the clubs had been apparent to him during his time ‌in England. “I think Man City should be punished severely. I think they should have to go down, and by the way, everyone knew about it. Everyone knew,” Marsch told The Guardian in an interview published on Sunday. Marsch also pointed to the 2022 summer transfer window, when Leeds sold Raphinha to Barcelona and Kalvin Phillips to City, while both clubs reported making money. “That summer [2022], us and Man City were the only teams that said ⁠we made money,” he said. “For us, we did make money, because we ⁠sold Raphinha, we sold Kalvin Phillips. We had a lot left over from what we bought. “At the time, we weren’t in a position financially to not save. Our ownership didn’t have deep pockets. Whereas when ⁠Man City says this, I was literally like, ‘Are you kidding me? Is this some kind of joke?'” The American coach was also sceptical about ⁠City’s signing of Erling Haaland from Borussia Dortmund that summer. Advertisement “When ⁠they said they got Erling Haaland for 52 million pounds ($69m), it’s like, ‘Yeah, OK, sure!’ So, I knew there were inconsistencies in it, but what can you do? You just put your arms in the air and go, ‘This is football’,” Marsch said. City’s appeal will be heard privately by an independent three-member board, with the club fully denying all charges. Potential sanctions include fines, points deductions and other sporting penalties, with relegation or ‌the ‌removal of titles also discussed as possible outcomes. title: Cristiano Ronaldo can return to Portugal team if he wants, says Jesus
body: Cristiano Ronaldo can return to Portugal team if he wants, says Jesus | Football | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Sport | Football Cristiano Ronaldo can return to Portugal team if he wants, says Jesus Ex-Manchester United and Real Madrid star Cristiano Ronaldo left the Portugal squad on Wednesday, but the door is open for his return. Listen Listen (4 mins) Save Share Cristiano Ronaldo can return to Portugal team if he wants, says Jesus on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo was relegated to the substitutes bench before his Nations League walkout [Lise Aserud/Reuters] By Kevin Hand and AFP Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 Portugal superstar Cristiano Ronaldo can return to the squad if he wishes, despite walking out on his teammates, national team coach Jorge Jesus said on Sunday. The Portuguese showed they did not need the former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward as they became the first side to qualify for the quarterfinals of the 2026-27 UEFA Nations League with a 2-1 comeback win against Norway. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Ronaldo-less Portugal beat Norway 2-1 to reach Nations League quarterfinals list 2 of 4 Fernandes calls Ronaldo and denies Portugal rift ahead of Norway game list 3 of 4 Portugal coach responds after Ronaldo leaves camp list 4 of 4 Why did Ronaldo leave Portugal’s training camp, and will he play again? end of list Goncalo Ramos secured the victory for his side in the 86th minute after Joao Cancelo’s powerful finish had levelled Kristoffer Ajer’s stunning opener from outside the penalty area for World Cup quarterfinalists Norway. After the game, Jesus said he was prepared to allow 41-year-old Ronaldo to return to the national team but that it would have to be the player’s decision. “For me, Cris, in the next call-up, if he’s playing at Al-Nassr, he’ll be a player who can be called up,” Jesus told reporters, referring to Ronaldo’s Saudi club side. “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team.” The coach said he would speak with Ronaldo if he wished before Portugal’s next matches in November. “If he wants to, as we did before this call-up, we talked before the call-up; we can talk before the next call-up,” continued Jesus. “But Cris is the one who’s going to decide.” Ronaldo walked out of the national-team camp on Wednesday after a dispute over his selection by Jesus, leaving his international future in doubt. Portugal’s leading goalscorer and most-capped player, Ronaldo was substituted in the Nations League opener against Wales on September 24. Advertisement He was then an unused substitute in the 2-1 victory in Norway on September 27. When he was informed he would again be named on the bench for the match in Denmark, Ronaldo took a private flight back to Saudi Arabia. Portugal went on to win 4-2 in Denmark on Thursday, while rumours swirled about Ronaldo’s departure and whether he would play for the national team again. Ronaldo’s international teammate, Bruno Fernandes, spoke to the media on Saturday in the buildup to the return match against Norway in an attempt to settle a growing furore in Portugal about the matter. “He has a reserved place not only among the best of all time, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people, and the most important thing is that we stop dividing things,” Fernandes said. “There are no divisions in the national team. It is one and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside… “We are outside of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country does not divide itself, does not make choices, that it respects all sides, but at the same time, Cris is and will be the biggest icon of our national team; he deserves everyone’s respect, regardless of who likes him more or [who likes him] less.” Jesus had said he would speak about Ronaldo after Sunday’s match with Norway, but added in the buildup to the game that the forward is a “symbol of Portugal”. The 72-year-old coach went on to say on Sunday that he had told Ronaldo he needed him in the squad for his first games at the helm after replacing Roberto Martinez following the 2026 World Cup. “Cristiano should end his time in the national team the way he wants; he’s the one who will decide how he wants it,” Jesus said. “That’s how we talked, the two of us – I said, ‘I need you’. In my first call-up, I said, ‘I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you’. And now I’m saying the same thing.” Ronaldo, who made his Portugal debut in 2003 at the age of 18, has said this will “probably” be his final year in football. The forward has been a fixture of the national team for more than two decades and has played at six World Cups. Portugal host Denmark in their next international on November 14, before completing their Nations League group in Wales on November 17. Ronaldo’s longtime rival for the title of the world’s best player, Lionel Messi, will play his final match for Argentina in a friendly against Benin in Buenos Aires on Tuesday. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network

body: Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Bosnia and Herzegovina Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election Jon Shelton | Dharvi Vaid Dhulia with AFP, AP, DPA and Reuters Published 10/04/2026 Published October 4, 2026 last updated 10/05/2026 last updated October 5, 2026 Bosnia-Herzegovina's three-member presidency is set to be dominated by nationalists from the three major ethnic groups, including Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, backed by disqualified Serb secessionist leader Milorad Dodik. https://p.dw.com/p/5Nim0 Preliminary results show strong results for ethnic-nationalist blocs Image: Armin Durgut/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Bosnian officials reported a record-low turnout following the Sunday vote, with only 41.5% out of the country's 3.4 million voters taking part in the general election in Bosnia-Herzegovina . Nationalist parties dominated races as citizens chose officials across multiple tiers of government; including members of the country's multiethnic, tripartite presidency. With counting nearly concluded, Serb nationalist Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, Bosniak moderate leftist Denis Becirovic and Croat nationalist ‌Darijana ​Filipovic have been announced as the winners of the presidential seats of their respective ethnicities. Cvijanovic had been backed by the Republika Srpska's former secessionist leader ​ Milorad Dodik , who was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process. "I am declaring that we have won," Dodik told supporters in Banja Luka on Sunday night. He said his SNSD party had retained the Serb seat in the presidency and remained power in Republika Srpska. Voters queued in Banja Luka and other cities around the country Image: Radivoje Pavicic/AP Photo/picture alliance With counting nearly over, Cvijanovic looked to have won with 55.6% of the vote. Social Democrat Becirovic won the race for the Bosniak seat with 38.1% of the vote, while Croat Filipovic took 48.2% of the vote. Nationalist and ethnic political division Voters also chose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and the Serb-run Republika Srpska (RS). Currently, about 50% of Bosnia and Herzegovina's citizens are Muslim Bosniaks, 31% are Orthodox Serb and another 15% are Catholic Croat. Between 1992 and 1995, more than two million people were displaced and nearly 100,000 killed in a civil war. Despite the country being peaceful for decades, ethnonationalist parties have kept divisions alive as a way to hold on to power. Many voters, however, say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric. The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges. There's been an economic downturn, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and sustained political gridlock — with dominant ethnic parties from these entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that binds them. The election saw contests that pitted the Bosniak ​SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party. Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results to be released later in the evening — though complex constitutional order and drawn out coalition talks mean that the true result of Sunday's election could remain unclear for months. What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina? The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the two semi-autonomous entities FBiH and RS, and the self-governing neutral Brcko district. These entities are further split into several cantons and communities. The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords , following the 1992-95 Bosnian war, itself a consequence of the breakup of Yugoslavia. Milorad Dodik still powerful figure in Republika Srpska In Republika Srpska , secessionist leader ​ Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remained the key figure of the election despite not being on the ballot. Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process. Dodik-backed Savo Minic decisively won the Republika Srpska's presidency and RS increased its heft by taking 39% of the parliamentary tally, up from 34.6% in 2022. After the vote, Dodik, who just returned from meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, thanked Putin and also credited "Donald Trump's magnificent victory" for keeping his political camp alive. He added that "now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners." Dodik, wants close ‌ties to Serbia and Russia and secession from Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday. What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina? In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state. The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism. Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union. Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO. Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022. But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption ​laws. title: Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws
body: Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws | Education News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Education Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws New York lawmakers will review sexual-assault laws, including the ‘voluntary intoxication’ rule at the heart of the Cornell case. Listen Listen (9 mins) Save Share Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info A poster advertises an upcoming protest for sexual assault prevention at Cornell University in the US on October 1 [Lauren Petracca/Reuters] By Catherine Nouhan Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 Last month, a woman identified as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against Cornell University, the fraternity Chi Phi and the seven fraternity members she accused of gang-raping her on the night of October 19, 2024. Her allegations have triggered a nationwide reckoning in the United States over the prevalence of sexual assault on college campuses. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Cornell rape allegations renew push to change New York sexual assault law list 2 of 3 ‘I want the truth’: NY governor appoints prosecutor in Cornell rape case list 3 of 3 Cornell president vows transparency amid outrage over fraternity rape case end of list But the case has also reignited efforts to reform laws in the state of New York. While the left-leaning state has long presented itself as a leader in women’s rights, advocates say sexual assault survivors still face pervasive legal barriers when they seek justice. Erica Vladimer, a lawyer and founding director of Harassment-Free New York, a survivor-led nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that much of the legislation currently in the spotlight is the culmination of years, if not decades, of work. “These are bills that we have been fighting for for years when sexual violence is not in the news,” Vladimer said. She drew a line between the #MeToo movement, which began in 2017 as an online campaign to denounce sexual misconduct, and the current wave of outrage following Doe’s allegations. “It speaks to the fact that the #MeToo movement is not dead. It is a movement, not a moment,” Vladimer said. Already, leaders in Albany, the state capital, have signalled they would take action following the Cornell case. On Wednesday, the New York Assembly announced it had formed a working group to examine the state’s sexual-assault laws and develop recommendations for the 2027 legislative session. Advertisement Still, advocates say more concrete measures are needed to address the crisis. “I appreciate that this work is happening,” said Lindsey Boylan, a New York City Council candidate. “It doesn’t undo the fact that rape culture is pervasive in the United States and very much so alive and well in New York.” Boylan was the first woman to publicly accuse former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo of sexual harassment in another high-profile misconduct case, back in 2020. She is among those calling for greater reform. Here are some of the measures advocates are pushing state lawmakers to adopt or amend: ‘Voluntary intoxication’ statute The Cornell University case has brought renewed attention to New York’s “ voluntary intoxication ” statute, a legal loophole that can make it harder to prosecute sexual assault when a person has willingly consumed alcohol or drugs. New York Governor Kathy Hochul pledged on Friday to work with lawmakers to close the gap. “It should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” Hochul said. Under the current state law, a person who voluntarily drinks or takes drugs is not considered “mentally incapacitated” during an assault, even if they become too intoxicated to consent. That can make it harder for prosecutors to bring a sex-crime charge. The law primarily recognises incapacitation in the context of sexual assault when a person was involuntarily intoxicated, unconscious or otherwise “physically helpless”. That distinction has become central to the Cornell case. Doe has acknowledged that she consumed substances before the alleged rape, saying that she was pressured into drinking alcohol and taking the dissociative drug ketamine. The Tompkins County district attorney initially declined to bring charges, pointing to the law’s stance on “voluntary intoxication”. But the investigation has since been reopened, amid public pressure. New York is one of 19 states in the US that distinguish between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication when it comes to determining consent in sexual violence cases. But the Cornell case has spurred a push to remove the distinction from the law books. Critics have argued that sexual assault is no less grievous if a victim is drunk or has chosen to take drugs. “I mean, to have New York, a supposedly progressive state, penalise people who are sexually abused for drinking is disgusting,” Boylan told Al Jazeera. Vladimer, for her part, explained that distinguishing between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication as a means for pursuing sexual assault cases shifts the focus onto the actions of victims, rather than perpetrators. Advertisement “We essentially have codified victim-blaming by saying if you become voluntarily intoxicated and then are sexually assaulted, you essentially cannot seek justice in our court system,” Vladimer told Al Jazeera. In June, the New York state Senate unanimously passed a bill to allow sexual assault charges regardless of whether a victim is intoxicated voluntarily or involuntarily. But the legislation has yet to be taken up in the state Assembly. Students look on at Cornell University’s campus in Ithaca, New York, on October 1 [Lauren Petracca/Reuters] The rape-shield gap New York’s rape-shield protections limit the use of evidence about a complainant’s sexual history and conduct in criminal proceedings. But those protections do not currently extend to civil cases. This distinction could matter in the Cornell case because Doe filed a civil lawsuit. Vladimer said questions about a survivor’s behaviour could come up in the discovery process of a civil case, as well as in court. “There is the potential of her having to face questions about things like her sexual history,” Vladimer said. Bridie Farrell, the director of victim rights advocacy and legislation at the law firm Weitz and Luxenberg, told Al Jazeera that she has seen major differences in how male and female survivors are questioned in civil cases where this practice is still permitted. In one case involving a brother and sister who were both sexually assaulted, Farrell said the man was not questioned about his sexual history while the woman was “grilled on it”. A bill sponsored by State Senator Liz Krueger would extend rape-shield protections to civil proceedings. The measure passed the Senate in June and is currently before the Assembly Judiciary Committee. A student walks through an archway at Myron Taylor Hall on the Cornell University campus in Ithaca, New York, on October 1 [Lauren Petracca/Reuters] Retaliatory defamation lawsuits Advocates are also pushing for legislation to prevent retaliatory defamation lawsuits. Boylan said she has spent more than $2m defending herself in legal proceedings connected to her accusations against Cuomo, who stepped down as New York governor in 2021. He has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing, despite a state attorney general’s report that concluded he “engaged in conduct constituting sexual harassment”. “Every step of the way, we have a system that penalises people for speaking up about their own harm,” Boylan said. Boylan and Charlotte Bennett, a former aide who also accused Cuomo of sexual harassment, are proponents of the Speak Your Truth Act, which would provide legal protections for people who publicly report sexual assault, harassment or discrimination. The bill, sponsored by Assembly member Jessica Gonzalez-Rojas, would make certain communications about sexual assault, harassment or discrimination privileged when they are made without malice. It would also allow survivors of sexual misconduct who successfully defend themselves against a defamation lawsuit to recover legal fees and costs. The bill remains in an Assembly committee. Cornell University and local officials in Ithaca, New York, have faced questions about how they handled the Jane Doe case [Lauren Petracca/Reuters] A recent win, a long way to go For Bridie Farrell, the victims’ rights advocate, the fight for legal change is personal. Advertisement Farrell was a 15-year-old competitive speed skater in 1997 when she said she was sexually abused by her 33-year-old teammate and mentor. She came forward with her story of abuse in 2013. By then, the statute of limitations in her case had expired. Farrell later became an advocate for changes to New York’s laws, helping to pass the Child Victims Act in 2019 that extended the time available for survivors of childhood sexual abuse to pursue criminal and civil claims. The law allowed Farrell to file her own case, which she did in 2020. She tells Al Jazeera that a trial has finally been scheduled for June 2027. “Before we passed the Child Victims Act in 2019, New York was one of the worst in the country,” Farrell said of the situation for sexual assault survivors seeking justice. Farrell considers the legal impediments to Doe’s case — like the “voluntary intoxication” statute — all too predictable. “I’m not surprised if we haven’t updated a law that is archaic,” she said. Still, lawmakers have signalled willingness to reform such laws. In announcing the state Assembly’s working group on sexual-assault laws, Speaker Carl Heastie pledged to “thoughtfully” consider how the state can strengthen its laws. “The allegations being reported out of Cornell University are truly horrifying,” Heastie said on Wednesday. “We want to do everything we can to ensure victims of sexual assault see justice served.” But survivors and sexual violence advocates say the Cornell case points to problems that go beyond any single law. They hope to see widespread systemic and societal change. “Changing legislation is incredibly important. But legislation in a lot of cases can only go [as far as] the paper that it’s written on,” Boylan said. “It would be amiss to orient this horrible, tragic, unacceptable, infuriating case in isolation without looking at the broader rape culture of our state and our country.” aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network

body: Ireland refuse handshake with Israel and don armbands in Nations League tie | Football News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Navigation menu caret-left Israel-Palestine conflict Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons ‘This is an apartheid regime’ Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? History of flotilla campaigns caret-right Sport | Football Ireland refuse handshake with Israel and don armbands in Nations League tie Republic of Ireland football players again wear black armbands and refuse handshakes with Israel in UEFA Nations League. Listen Listen (5 mins) Save Share Ireland refuse handshake with Israel and don armbands in Nations League tie on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Irish players bow their heads during the Israeli national anthem before the UEFA Nations League match [Darko Vojinovic/AP] By Kevin Hand and The Associated Press Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 Ireland players again wore black armbands in recognition of Palestinians killed in Gaza and bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem before the teams’ second UEFA Nations League football match on Sunday. The League 3 Group B match ended in a 1-1 draw and, despite being played behind closed doors and on neutral ground, was once again played out in a confrontational manner. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 ‘Everyone knew’: Canada boss Marsch wants Man City relegated for breaches list 2 of 4 Cristiano Ronaldo can return to Portugal team if he wants, says Jesus list 3 of 4 Man City whistleblower Pinto says he ‘received death threats’ over leaks list 4 of 4 No handshakes and a delayed ceremony as India beat Pakistan at Asian Games end of list Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher stepped in as captain for Dara O’Shea, who was excused to be with his wife for the birth of their child, and pointedly avoided shaking hands with Israel captain Dor Peretz, despite completing the usual pre-match formality with the referee and one of his assistants. Kelleher’s action was a repeat of O’Shea’s, who refused to shake Israel captain Manor Solomon’s hand before the first match in Debrecen, Hungary, last week. Ireland went on to win that game 3-0 through three first-half goals. Solomon was dropped to the bench for Sunday’s match in Backa Topola, Serbia. Israel forward Sayed Abu Farchi was back in the squad after serving a suspension for getting sent off following his gun-simulation goal celebration during Israel’s 3-1 defeat to Austria on September 25. Finn Azaz, whose mother has Israeli heritage, was among the Irish substitutes after playing from the start against Austria on Thursday. Troy Parrott’s penalty in the 39th minute, after a foul by Peretz on Jimmy Dunne, gave Ireland a 1-0 halftime lead. A disagreement also broke out on the sidelines as the players made their way off the field for the interval, although the referee quickly intervened. Advertisement Peretz secured a point for Israel with a poked effort from close range in the 47th minute. Sunday’s game was initially supposed to be played in Dublin, but the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) moved it to a neutral venue for “operational reasons” in June following widespread calls for a boycott in protest of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The FAI said the game would be played with no fans present. It followed the FAI’s motion the previous November calling on UEFA to ban Israel from club and international competitions. All the Irish players had been under pressure from home – where affinity with Palestinians is strong – to boycott the second match against Israel, though the pressure was greater during the first game. “I felt that pressure growing day by day, and it’s getting almost to a breaking limit now,” Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said at the time. Ultimately, only reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu decided to skip both of the contentious games, saying in a statement that it was his “personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong”. More than 160 Irish sportspeople had signed an open letter urging the FAI to reconsider its decision to go ahead with the two games. Before the departure for Hungary, people protested outside the team hotel in Dublin for the players to boycott the matches. The SIPTU trade union displayed a huge poster in central Dublin beside the River Liffey asking the players to “Go with your conscience!” and “Don’t play with genocide” beside an image of a blood-splattered ball. Former Ireland coach Brian Kerr said the FAI had “lost the respect of the Irish people” for going ahead with the games. But the FAI argued UEFA could sanction the team. Ireland is cohosting the 2028 European Championship with England, Wales and Scotland. Protesters threw tennis balls with Palestinian flags onto the field during Ireland’s 2-2 draw with Austria on Thursday. A man with a Palestinian flag also tried running onto the field. On Saturday, an Israeli journalist stated during the pre-match news conference that the Irish players had called the Israeli players “monkeys” during last week’s game, leading to an immediate rebuke from Irish communications officer Kieran Crowley, who said it was “a lie” and ended the news conference. The players had only decided to go ahead with the fixtures after a dramatic day in Debrecen before the first match, when both the news conference and training were delayed for hours while they deliberated. They reportedly voted 14-8 in favour of continuing after Bazunu’s withdrawal that morning. Advertisement Ireland’s national broadcaster RTÉ was only providing stripped-back coverage of both games against Israel to meet contractual obligations. There was no studio presentation, commentary on the international feed, or analysis. RTÉ said it was not accepting advertising or sponsorship around either game.
