title: Brazil election: Early count puts Bolsonaro ahead of Lula
body: Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Brazil Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff Dmytro Hubenko | Wesley Rahn with Reuters, AFP, AP Published 10/04/2026 Published October 4, 2026 last updated 10/05/2026 last updated October 5, 2026 Populist Flavio Bolsonaro has secured a thin lead over incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but the next president of Brazil will be decided in the runoff round, according to the country’s electoral court. https://p.dw.com/p/5NiO9 The early count in the Brazilian presidential election puts Flavio Bolsonaro (left) ahead of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva Image: Alexandre Meneghini/Pilar Olivares/REUTERS Advertisement With votes being counted in Brazil following the presidential election on Sunday, populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro was leading the race ahead of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro seeks to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro, while Lula is seeking his fourth non-consecutive term. Commenting on the outcome, Lula said they were "unexpected" as he was convinced he would "win in the first round." "We are in extra time," the 80-year-old said. "In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people." With more than 99% of the ballots processed, Flavio Bolsonaro has received 47.2% of the vote. Lula has 45%, according to the electoral court. Since neither candidate received enough votes to win outright on Sunday, the court announced that Bolsonaro and Lula will face each other in a runoff. Bolsonaro is monitoring the vote count in Brasilia, the country's capital, while Lula is following it from Sao Paulo. Because Brazil uses electronic voting machines, final results are expected to be available within several hours of the polls closing. You can watch our livestream on the Brazil election results below. Right gaining momentum in Brazil Fabio de Sa e Silva, a professor of Brazilian studies at the University of Oklahoma, told DW that the right was currently on the rise in Brazil, making it difficult for Lula to change the course of the election. "He still has a chance, based on the numbers, but the momentum is with the right," said de Sa e Silva. "The big news tomorrow will be not that we have a runoff... but it is a takeover that happened in Congress by the far-right," the researcher said. He added that it will be very hard for Lula to govern with Brazil's new Congress, even if he eventually secures another term. Lula vows to 'defeat the far right' Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo. Long queues of voters were seen in parts of Rio de Janeiro Image: Bruna Prado/AP Photo/picture alliance The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right ." Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city. Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution. "The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday. The 80-year-old Lula is seeking the presidency for a fourth and final time Image: Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS Bolsonaro calls for 'change' Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana. He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him. Flavio Bolsonaro has said he would pardon his father if elected Image: Douglas Shineidr/AFP The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent." "Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed." Brazil's 2022 election rematch The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected. Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump , who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial.  The US president called the case a "witch hunt." Brazilians vote in high-stakes presidential election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference." Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change. Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely." US President Trump had held close ties with fellow right-wing populist Jair Bolsonaro [FILE March 2019] Image: Chris Kleponis/CNP/MediaPunch/picture alliance What happens next? Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media. In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct. Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency. In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%. In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points. Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators. title: Brazil: Polls close in tight race between Lula and Bolsonaro
body: Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Brazil Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff Dmytro Hubenko | Wesley Rahn with Reuters, AFP, AP Published 10/04/2026 Published October 4, 2026 last updated 10/05/2026 last updated October 5, 2026 Populist Flavio Bolsonaro has secured a thin lead over incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but the next president of Brazil will be decided in the runoff round, according to the country’s electoral court. https://p.dw.com/p/5NiO9 The early count in the Brazilian presidential election puts Flavio Bolsonaro (left) ahead of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva Image: Alexandre Meneghini/Pilar Olivares/REUTERS Advertisement With votes being counted in Brazil following the presidential election on Sunday, populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro was leading the race ahead of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro seeks to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro, while Lula is seeking his fourth non-consecutive term. Commenting on the outcome, Lula said they were "unexpected" as he was convinced he would "win in the first round." "We are in extra time," the 80-year-old said. "In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people." With more than 99% of the ballots processed, Flavio Bolsonaro has received 47.2% of the vote. Lula has 45%, according to the electoral court. Since neither candidate received enough votes to win outright on Sunday, the court announced that Bolsonaro and Lula will face each other in a runoff. Bolsonaro is monitoring the vote count in Brasilia, the country's capital, while Lula is following it from Sao Paulo. Because Brazil uses electronic voting machines, final results are expected to be available within several hours of the polls closing. You can watch our livestream on the Brazil election results below. Right gaining momentum in Brazil Fabio de Sa e Silva, a professor of Brazilian studies at the University of Oklahoma, told DW that the right was currently on the rise in Brazil, making it difficult for Lula to change the course of the election. "He still has a chance, based on the numbers, but the momentum is with the right," said de Sa e Silva. "The big news tomorrow will be not that we have a runoff... but it is a takeover that happened in Congress by the far-right," the researcher said. He added that it will be very hard for Lula to govern with Brazil's new Congress, even if he eventually secures another term. Lula vows to 'defeat the far right' Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo. Long queues of voters were seen in parts of Rio de Janeiro Image: Bruna Prado/AP Photo/picture alliance The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right ." Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city. Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution. "The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday. The 80-year-old Lula is seeking the presidency for a fourth and final time Image: Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS Bolsonaro calls for 'change' Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana. He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him. Flavio Bolsonaro has said he would pardon his father if elected Image: Douglas Shineidr/AFP The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent." "Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed." Brazil's 2022 election rematch The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected. Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump , who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial.  The US president called the case a "witch hunt." Brazilians vote in high-stakes presidential election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference." Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change. Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely." US President Trump had held close ties with fellow right-wing populist Jair Bolsonaro [FILE March 2019] Image: Chris Kleponis/CNP/MediaPunch/picture alliance What happens next? Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media. In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct. Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency. In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%. In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points. Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators. title: Polls close in Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election
body: Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Bosnia and Herzegovina Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election Jon Shelton | Dharvi Vaid Dhulia with AFP, AP, DPA and Reuters Published 10/04/2026 Published October 4, 2026 last updated 10/05/2026 last updated October 5, 2026 Bosnia-Herzegovina's three-member presidency is set to be dominated by nationalists from the three major ethnic groups, including Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, backed by disqualified Serb secessionist leader Milorad Dodik. https://p.dw.com/p/5Nim0 Preliminary results show strong results for ethnic-nationalist blocs Image: Armin Durgut/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Bosnian officials reported a record-low turnout following the Sunday vote, with only 41.5% out of the country's 3.4 million voters taking part in the general election in Bosnia-Herzegovina . Nationalist parties dominated races as citizens chose officials across multiple tiers of government; including members of the country's multiethnic, tripartite presidency. With counting nearly concluded, Serb nationalist Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, Bosniak moderate leftist Denis Becirovic and Croat nationalist ‌Darijana ​Filipovic have been announced as the winners of the presidential seats of their respective ethnicities. Cvijanovic had been backed by the Republika Srpska's former secessionist leader ​ Milorad Dodik , who was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process. "I am declaring that we have won," Dodik told supporters in Banja Luka on Sunday night. He said his SNSD party had retained the Serb seat in the presidency and remained power in Republika Srpska. Voters queued in Banja Luka and other cities around the country Image: Radivoje Pavicic/AP Photo/picture alliance With counting nearly over, Cvijanovic looked to have won with 55.6% of the vote. Social Democrat Becirovic won the race for the Bosniak seat with 38.1% of the vote, while Croat Filipovic took 48.2% of the vote. Nationalist and ethnic political division Voters also chose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and the Serb-run Republika Srpska (RS). Currently, about 50% of Bosnia and Herzegovina's citizens are Muslim Bosniaks, 31% are Orthodox Serb and another 15% are Catholic Croat. Between 1992 and 1995, more than two million people were displaced and nearly 100,000 killed in a civil war. Despite the country being peaceful for decades, ethnonationalist parties have kept divisions alive as a way to hold on to power. Many voters, however, say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric. The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges. There's been an economic downturn, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and sustained political gridlock — with dominant ethnic parties from these entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that binds them. The election saw contests that pitted the Bosniak ​SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party. Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results to be released later in the evening — though complex constitutional order and drawn out coalition talks mean that the true result of Sunday's election could remain unclear for months. What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina? The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the two semi-autonomous entities FBiH and RS, and the self-governing neutral Brcko district. These entities are further split into several cantons and communities. The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords , following the 1992-95 Bosnian war, itself a consequence of the breakup of Yugoslavia. Milorad Dodik still powerful figure in Republika Srpska In Republika Srpska , secessionist leader ​ Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remained the key figure of the election despite not being on the ballot. Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process. Dodik-backed Savo Minic decisively won the Republika Srpska's presidency and RS increased its heft by taking 39% of the parliamentary tally, up from 34.6% in 2022. After the vote, Dodik, who just returned from meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, thanked Putin and also credited "Donald Trump's magnificent victory" for keeping his political camp alive. He added that "now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners." Dodik, wants close ‌ties to Serbia and Russia and secession from Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday. What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina? In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state. The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism. Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union. Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO. Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022. But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption ​laws. title: Indian police accused of sexual harassment against journalists at protest
body: Indian police accused of sexual harassment against journalists at protest - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat Asia China India Indian police accused of sexually harassing journalists at protest Image source, EPA Image caption, Young people have been protesting against large-scale changes to voter rolls by the Election Commission By Parul Gupta Published 4 October 2026 Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during street protests in the capital Delhi. The claims were made on Saturday after the force detained scores of young people calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner. In a post on social media, Delhi Police said its New Delhi District had received the complaint, and it had been transferred to its crime branch for a "fair and impartial" inquiry. Thousands of protesters gathered in Delhi and Mumbai cities for a third day on Sunday demanding that Gyanesh Kumar step down over large-scale changes to voter rolls. The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list. Videos online show people being physically dragged away from the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi. The accusations by the women journalists include inappropriate touching by some police. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said women fear for their safety and the home ministry must "answer for this". "Police dragged me by my hair," Aahna Singh, an activist and student at Jawaharlal Nehru University told Reuters news agency during the protests. She said the police were resorting to "brutality". The Press Club of India has demanded immediate action on the complaints against police officers, saying it was "shocked and dismayed" by the treatment of journalists. "Behaviour of this kind cannot be normalised in a democracy. Journalists must be allowed to work freely, without fear, and document those who gather to raise various issues," it said in a statement. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Demonstrators scuffle with police during a protest in New Delhi over the alleged assault The protesters say the voter-roll revision will benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries. It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address. But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour the BJP during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations. The protesters have included supporters of the influential Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) that began as an online satirical movement. The pressure group recorded its first major victory in July when it forced the then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign after weeks of protests calling for education reforms. The CJP called for the latest protest after a report in The Indian Express , external said that Kumar's two fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge. The differences were reported to be mostly over the controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year. The Election Commission has defended its way of working and said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process" and that all the decisions were taken unanimously. But the revelations sparked a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation. title: Mass protests demanding poll chief resignation shake India for third day
body: Mass protests demanding poll chief resignation shake India for third day | Elections News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Elections Mass protests demanding poll chief resignation shake India for third day Protesters say the election commission’s voter-roll revision has removed millions of eligible voters to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling BJP party. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share Mass protests demanding poll chief resignation shake India for third day on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Protesters carry India’s national flag during a demonstration calling for the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the country’s chief election commissioner, over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls, in Mumbai on October 4, 2026 [Punit Paranjpe/AFP] By Al Jazeera Staff , AFP and Reuters Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 Thousands of youth and opposition protesters have rallied for a third day in India demanding the resignation of the country’s election commission chief. Thousands marched in Mumbai on Sunday, while others gathered for a third day of demonstrations in New Delhi. The protests began on Friday demanding that Election Commission of India (ECI) chief Gyanesh Kumar step down due to reports that he has overseen voter-roll revisions removing millions from electoral lists. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Dodik declared Bosnia ‘dead’. Irrelevant rhetoric or serious threat? list 2 of 3 Why is fighting intensifying in Yemen’s Taiz governorate? list 3 of 3 How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk? end of list Protesters say the disenfranchisement stands to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the ECI and the BJP have denied the allegations. Led by opposition leaders Raj Thackeray and Uddhav Thackeray, thousands marched in Mumbai on Sunday, waving Indian flags and calling for Kumar to step down. In the capital, New Delhi, protesters started gathering in the early evening. As on previous days, some were detained by police as they arrived, according to the Reuters news agency. Police in the capital have clamped down in a bid to prevent protesters from assembling over the last two days, detaining dozens and taking them away by bus. Some of the detainees were released later on Friday and Saturday, but police registered cases against some on charges of violating orders banning mass gatherings in the centre of the capital. Police and security personnel detain a protester during a demonstration against India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi on October 3, 2026, to demand his resignation [Arun Sankar/AFP] “⁠I just want to tell the ruling party this much … We are angry about how you are wielding that power. ⁠It’s the people of this country who should decide who sits in power and who sits in opposition, not the election commission,” Raj Thackeray told the crowd in Mumbai. Advertisement The ECI says the voter-roll revision is designed to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible entries and maintain electoral integrity. On Friday, it directed its officials to register eligible voters inadvertently omitted from electoral rolls. Kumar has not publicly responded to the demands for his resignation or commented on the protests, which look set to continue over the coming days, with more rallies planned. An alliance of India’s opposition parties plans to launch protests to “save democracy” with a march to the election commission office on Tuesday. The Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has announced plans for a major rally in New Delhi on October 10. “Mumbai is out on the streets again for free and fair elections!” Abhijeet Dipke, chief of the CJP, said in a social media post on Sunday. “Solidarity with all the protesters,” he added. “All Indians need to come together. title: Yemen's government announces all-out war to reclaim land from Houthis
body: Yemen government announces major operation to retake Houthi territory - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Yemen's government announces all-out war to reclaim land from Houthis Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Soldiers ride in the back of a pick-up truck on a dirt road near Taiz, amid fighting between Yemeni government forces and Houthis By Sebastian Usher , Global affairs correspondent and Tinshui Yeung Published 4 October 2026 The head of Yemen's internationally recognised government has announced it will wage an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis. It follows an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in recent days. The Iran-backed group said it had struck sites belonging to Saudi national oil company Aramco, in response to what it described as 50 Saudi-led coalition strikes in 12 hours. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment. The Yemeni government's fierce statement was expected after the Houthis' offensive last month, which saw them seize control of the country's Red Sea coastline, including the vital shipping lane of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on 3 October On Sunday, Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address: "Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory." Yemen's capital, Sanaa, which has been held by the Houthis for more than a decade, has come under sustained attack as government forces try to weaken the group's military capabilities. Attacks on the Houthis have also spread across Yemen, including to the Saada region, the group's northern heartland. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi addresses the nation in a televised address in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia But security sources say the Iran-backed Houthis have continued to make gains. The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which is still controlled by the internationally recognised government. On Sunday, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government, AFP news agency reports. Citing three Yemeni military sources, AFP also reports that the Houthis now control the area and supply route, effectively encircling Taiz. "They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank, told AFP. Al-Alimi was unlikely to have made the announcement without the green light from Saudi Arabia, which remains the key backer of his government. Saudi Arabia has been under constant attack as the Houthis try to target the country's economic lifeblood - oil. On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east. "Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites." It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories". But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis. In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday. On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Smoke rises from the site of an air strike in Sanaa on 4 October Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis. A war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital city from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of swathes of the country's north. Riyadh intervened in the war the following year, leading an international coalition. After several years of relative calm, the war reignited in July amid the widening conflict in the Middle East. Last month, a lightning offensive enabled the Houthis to seize the country's entire Red Sea coast, stopping Saudi Arabia from using it as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz. The strategy benefited the Houthis' main sponsor, Iran. But it has also forced Saudi Arabia back into direct military confrontation with the Houthis. title: US and Man City’s Cavan Sullivan becomes youngest international goalscorer
body: Man City’s Cavan Sullivan becomes youngest US international goalscorer | Football | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up Sport | Football Man City’s Cavan Sullivan becomes youngest US international goalscorer Sullivan’s goal beat fellow teenager Julian Hall’s record for United States which was only set against Chile on Tuesday. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share Man City’s Cavan Sullivan becomes youngest US international goalscorer on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Cavan Sullivan is poised to join English Premier League side Manchester City next year [File: Rick Scuteri/AP] By AFP Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 Cavan Sullivan became the youngest US international goalscorer in history as the United States defeated archrivals Mexico 3-0 in a friendly international in Arizona on Saturday. Sullivan, who is poised to join English Premier League side Manchester City next year, netted a superbly taken goal in the 62nd minute to double the USA lead at the State Farm Stadium in Glendale. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Man City whistleblower Pinto says he ‘received death threats’ over leaks list 2 of 4 ‘Verbal attack’: Israeli reporters interrupt Ireland news conference list 3 of 4 Fernandes calls Ronaldo and denies Portugal rift ahead of Norway game list 4 of 4 Tributes as Bosnian football star Edin Dzeko retires end of list At 17 years and five days, Sullivan beat Mathis Albert’s five-day-old record as the youngest US goalscorer. Albert, aged 17 and 31 days, scored during Tuesday’s 4-2 defeat of Chile. “These are the moments you dream of when you’re three, four, five or six-years-old,” Sullivan said. “I manifested this moment, not just these past couple of hours when I found out I was starting, but my whole life,” he added. Sullivan’s strike came after another teenager — 18-year-old Julian Hall — had given Mauricio Pochettino’s side the lead in the 28th minute. Hall’s goal was his third in as many games since being handed his international debut by US coach Pochettino in last week’s defeat of Peru. Hall also scored in the victory over Chile. The loss puts more pressure on Mexico coach Rafael Marquez, who is still seeking his first win since taking over following the World Cup. Mexico dominated possession and territory early on but were unable to find a way through a well-organised United States defence. Instead, it was the hosts who took the lead just before the half-hour mark with a superbly worked goal from Hall. Gio Reyna surged into the penalty area to collect a pass from Alex Freeman and ghosted past Mexico midfielder Erik Lira to reach the byline. Advertisement Reyna’s low cross was parried away by Mexico goalkeeper Raul Rangel, but only as far as Hall, who lashed in from close range to make it 1-0. Mexico’s best chance came early in the second half when Roberto Alvarado’s rasping shot from the edge of the area was tipped over the bar by US goalkeeper Diego Kochen. Pochettino’s side doubled their lead on 62 minutes when Sullivan’s persistence in chasing down a long ball was rewarded after Rangel mishit a pass to the American outside his area. Sullivan coolly took his time and chipped home from long range to make it 2-0. “I just remember chipping the ball, hoping it didn’t hit the crossbar or go over,” Sullivan said of his strike. “I was getting nervous when it was in the air and then everything was a blur.” A miserable night for Mexico got worse shortly afterwards when substitute Luis Chavez was shown a red card for shoving a hand into the face of Sebastian Berhalter in the 68th minute. The United States completed the scoring in the 84th minute when Malik Tillman latched onto a poor Mexico backpass and smashed a shot into the top corner for 3-0. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network

body: Philippines arrests 244 suspects in online scam crackdown | Human Trafficking News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Human Trafficking Philippines arrests 244 suspects in online scam crackdown Criminal gangs accused of using Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) as cover for human trafficking, fraud, murder. Listen Listen (3 mins) Save Share Philippines arrests 244 suspects in online scam crackdown on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Military and other law enforcement agencies in the Philippines raided several addresses in Mindanao [File: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images] By Al Jazeera Staff and AFP Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 Philippine authorities have arrested more than 200 foreign workers, mostly Chinese, in their biggest crackdown this year on illegal offshore gaming operators. The country’s Immigration Bureau reported late on Saturday that military and other law enforcement agencies had raided two addresses on the southern Philippine island of Mindanao on Friday. Criminal gangs are accused of using Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) as cover for various crimes. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Duterte in person at ICC for first time over ‘war on drugs’ killings list 2 of 4 Philippines school shooting leaves at least three dead, including gunman list 3 of 4 Chinese ship rams Philippines gov’t vessel in South China Sea: Coastguard list 4 of 4 Thousands of drivers strike in the Philippines over rising fuel prices end of list The raid on one site resulted in the arrest of 110 Chinese citizens, two Cambodians and a Hong Kong resident, according to the bureau’s statement. A further 131 foreign citizens were arrested at the second site. Again, the majority were Chinese, alongside citizens of Malaysia, Indonesia and Myanmar, according to the statement. Authorities seized large quantities of computer equipment, mobile phones, laptops and SIM cards. Manila banned POGOs in 2024 on the grounds that crime groups use them as a cover for human trafficking , money laundering, kidnappings, fraud and murder. A 2023 United Nations report noted that in recent years hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked by gangs and forced to work in scam centres and other illegal online operations across Southeast Asia. The UN report estimated that at least 120,000 people across Myanmar and approximately 100,000 in Cambodia may be trapped in scam operations, with other criminal-owned enterprises in Laos, the Philippines and Thailand ranging from crypto-fraud to online gambling. Advertisement The Philippine government is investigating potential human trafficking-related offences by several of those arrested in the latest raids, while the rest will be deported. International concern has grown in recent years over similar scam operations in other Asian nations, where trafficking victims are tricked or coerced into promoting bogus cryptocurrency investments and other cons. “We will continue to enforce our immigration laws against foreign nationals who violate the conditions of their stay and ensure that the Philippines is not used as a base for illegal activities,” immigration chief Joel Viado said in the statement. Chinese embassy spokesperson Ji Lingpeng told the AFP news agency that they are “reaching out to the Philippine law enforcement agencies on the details of this case”. “Chinese law prohibits any form of gambling , including Chinese nationals gambling overseas or working for gambling companies,” he added. aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo Advertisement About About Show more About Us Code of Ethics Terms and Conditions EU/EEA Regulatory Notice Privacy Policy Cookie Policy Cookie Preferences Accessibility Statement Sitemap Work for us Connect Connect Show more Contact Us User Accounts Help Advertise with us Stay Connected Newsletters Channel Finder TV Schedule Podcasts Submit a Tip Paid Partner Content Our Channels Our Channels Show more Al Jazeera Arabic Al Jazeera English Al Jazeera Investigative Unit Al Jazeera Mubasher Al Jazeera Documentary Al Jazeera Balkans AJ+ Our Network Our Network Show more Al Jazeera Centre for Studies Al Jazeera Media Institute Learn Arabic Al Jazeera Centre for Public Liberties & Human Rights Al Jazeera Forum Al Jazeera Hotel Partners Follow Al Jazeera English: facebook twitter youtube instagram-colored-outline rss bluesky tiktok-colored-outline © 2026 Al Jazeera Media Network

title: Why is fighting intensifying in Yemen’s Taiz governorate?
body: Why is fighting intensifying in Yemen’s Taiz governorate? | Conflict News | Al Jazeera Skip links Skip to Content play Live Sign up Show navigation menu Navigation menu News Show more news sections Africa Asia US & Canada Latin America Europe Asia Pacific Middle East Explained Sport Opinion Video More Show more sections Originals Features Economy Human Rights Climate Crisis Investigations Interactives In Pictures Science & Technology Podcasts Travel Sponsored Content play Live Click here to search search Sign up News | Conflict Why is fighting intensifying in Yemen’s Taiz governorate? Government forces fend off waves of Houthi attacks as civilians in the populous province are imperiled. Listen Listen (6 mins) Save Share Why is fighting intensifying in Yemen’s Taiz governorate? on social media share-nodes Share facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Damaged buildings in Taiz City, capital of the Taiz governorate in southwestern Yemen, on September 25, 2026 [AFP] By Al Jazeera Staff Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-backed Houthis are engaged in a fierce struggle for the Taiz governorate, a key strategic area in the southwest of the country. Rashad al-Alimi, chief of the Saudi Arabia-backed Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced on Sunday the start of a major offensive against the Houthis to regain lost territory. It is expected that this will result in more battles around Taiz, already the site of some of the most recent fighting. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 A Yemeni family spends a week on the road fleeing another Houthi offensive list 2 of 4 Yemen’s war disrupts roads and ports, deepening humanitarian crisis list 3 of 4 Yemen’s army says targets Houthis in hundreds of strikes, killing 700 list 4 of 4 Saudi-led coalition dismisses ‘misleading’ Houthi claim of Riyadh attack end of list Observers and analysts say that the Houthis are trying to consolidate their gains after seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month. For the government, the battle for Taiz represents a strategic and existential struggle for control of the country. Here’s what we know. Why is Taiz important? Taiz governorate is Yemen’s most populous region, with nearly 4.5 million people. The flat western coastal region sits on the Red Sea and includes the port city of Mocha and the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait. These coastal regions were captured by the Houthis in a surprise and lightning campaign in early September, raising fears the group could choke off international shipping through the strait. They were also key supply routes for Taiz. Much of the governorate lies within Yemen’s highlands and remains contested between the two sides. The region’s capital, Taiz City, is nestled between a number of mountains and is under government control. It is one of Yemen’s most populous cities and a key source of legitimacy for the Yemeni government. Advertisement The governorate sits between Yemen’s Houthi-controlled north and the government-held south. The Houthi advance threatens to isolate government forces from Aden, the southern coastal town where key state institutions are based. Ibrahim Jalal, a senior researcher and policy adviser, told Al Jazeera that Taiz is a city of huge social, political, economic and military importance for the whole of Yemen. “The Houthi attempt to isolate and constrict the city seeks to secure their coastal Red Sea gains up to Bab al-Mandeb, as well as double down on pressure on Lahij, Aden and much of the south,” said Jalal. “The Houthis seek to expand their territorial control at the moment along the former boundaries of northern Yemen, or to say, that they want to remove all little pockets of resistance to consolidate control.” Taiz has been one of the most heavily contested cities in the war, beginning shortly after Houthi forces captured the capital Sanaa in September 2014. Thousands of civilians have been killed in a devastating Houthi siege and assault on the city, with government forces driving back repeated assaults between 2015 and 2022. Map showing territorial control in Yemen’s civil war as of September 30, 2026 [Al Jazeera] Fighting has been focused on Jabal Han, a mountain overlooking Taiz from the west, as well as a key road into the city. Control over this mountain would allow the Houthis to attack people and supplies entering Taiz City from the southwest, Saeed Thabet, head of Al Jazeera’s bureau in Yemen, said. Who has the upper hand? There has been no clear winner in the battle for Taiz so far, which observers have described as a stalemate. Al Jazeera’s Mohammed al-Qadi, reporting from the city, said government forces have launched dozens of air strikes on Houthi bases and positions across Taiz in recent days. Houthi fighters are trying to advance under cover of intense artillery, tank, mortar and Katyusha rocket fire into the city. Artillery fire could be heard around Taiz as residents appealed to be evacuated, Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz City, said on Sunday. On that day, local authorities reported that a shell had hit a residential area in Dhubab, killing a 14-day-old infant. Other attacks have wounded civilians. Government forces are also shelling Houthi forces positioned around the city. Face-to-face fighting has now reached the countryside on the outskirts of Taiz City. Residents are fighting on their own initiative against Houthi attempts to infiltrate villages and mountain areas around Taiz, a local source said. The heaviest fighting is taking place at the western axis of the city, where government forces have mounted a fierce defence at Jabal Han. Advertisement On Sunday, Yemen’s government forces announced gains against the Houthis, saying they had captured several areas, including a fort in Samaa. The military command in Taiz also claimed its forces had repelled Houthi attacks on Jabal Han, Hazran and other points west of Taiz City. Yemeni military spokesman Majed al-Nuzaili said government forces had carried out dozens of operations using aircraft, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers, resulting in hundreds of Houthi casualties. Al Jazeera could not verify these claims. In early September, the Houthis managed to expand their control over Yemen’s Red Sea coast with unexpected speed and limited resistance. However, they have faced much fiercer fighting from government forces in Taiz. One key reason for this is the cohesion between government forces and the local tribes. Al Jazeera’s Yasser Hassan reports that tribesmen took part in Sunday’s capture of the Samaa Fort. How are civilians in Taiz being impacted? The humanitarian cost of the renewed fighting in Taiz has already manifested in a refugee crisis with limited access to humanitarian goods and services. There has also been an increase in civilian casualties. Since fighting escalated in early September, nearly 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen, most of them from Taiz governorate, according to Yemen’s Executive Unit for IDP Camps Management. The closure of some major roads into Taiz City has raised fears of an impending humanitarian disaster. Saudi-backed Yemeni government soldiers gather near the Jabal Han front, west of Taiz City, on October 3, 2026 [Ahmed Al-Basha/AFP] The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the World Health Organization (WHO) have both warned that the fighting was putting Yemen’s fragile healthcare system in peril. Al Jazeera’s Hassan described the humanitarian situation as “very difficult” after government forces decided to shut down all roads leading into the city out of fear of Houthi infiltration. Before Mocha was taken over by Houthis, its port was a critical supply line from which food and aid were delivered to Taiz City. The ongoing war has also devastated the country. title: Sports betting is increasingly the norm for Gen Z.  Here’s why some financial and mental health experts are worried
body:
Gen Z sports betting: Financial and mental health risks Skip Navigation Markets Pre-Markets U.S. Markets Currencies Prediction Markets Cryptocurrency Futures & Commodities Bonds Funds & ETFs Business Economy Finance Health & Science Media Real Estate Energy Climate Transportation Investigations Industrials Retail Wealth Sports Life Small Business Investing Personal Finance Fintech Financial Advisors Options Action ETF Street Buffett Archive Earnings Trader Talk Tech Cybersecurity AI Enterprise Internet Media Mobile Social Media CNBC Disruptor 50 Tech Guide Politics & Policy White House Policy Defense Congress Expanding Opportunity Video Latest Video Full Episodes Livestream Live Audio Live TV Schedule CNBC Podcasts CEO Interviews CNBC Documentaries Digital Originals Watchlist Investing Club Trust Portfolio Analysis Trade Alerts Meeting Videos Homestretch Jim's Columns Education Subscribe PRO Pro News Josh Brown Mike Santoli Calls of the Day My Portfolio Livestream Full Episodes Stock Screener Market Forecast Options Investing Chart Investing Subscribe Livestream Menu Make It select USA INTL Livestream Search quotes, news & videos Livestream Watchlist SIGN IN Create free account Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Markets Sports betting is increasingly the norm for Gen Z.  Here’s why some financial and mental health experts are worried Published Sun, Oct 4 2026 8:57 AM EDT Davis Giangiulio @in/davis-giangiulio @GiangiulioDavis WATCH LIVE Key Points Since the rise of online sportsbooks and now the introduction of prediction markets, Gen Z is increasingly wagering on sports outcomes. But surveys show some members of the generation view the bets as investments, despite the fact that users on average lose money on these platforms. Those who bet and lose the most are at greater risk for developing gambling problems, which clinicians anecdotally report are increasing among young people. The Draft Kings website arranged on a laptop in New Hyde Park, New York, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 17, 2025. Gabby Jones | Bloomberg | Getty Images Wagering on sports outcomes has exploded in the 2020s , but recent surveys show just how widespread gambling has become for Generation Z . A survey of retail investors released in August by Betterment, an investment advisory platform, found that 66% of Gen Z investors participate in sports betting. The Bank of America Institute found in a September report that Gen Z made up almost 50% of all online betting activity in July , during the height of the 2026 FIFA World Cup , outnumbering millennials for the first time. "It is more unusual for someone not to have, for example, a Kalshi account, DraftKings … than it is" to have such an account, said Cynthia Grant, vice president of clinical at Birches Health, which provides online therapy for online gambling addiction recovery. "It's part of the experience of watching sports now." Sports betting surged after a 2018 U.S. Supreme Court allowing state-authorized sportsbooks, which have since spread to 30 states. The introduction of sports-related event contracts on prediction markets — which claim they are financial trades, not wagers — in early 2025 further expanded access to additional states without legalized sportsbooks, and to those under 21. Now, the proliferation of sports betting has many financial and mental health advisors on edge. The average user on both a sportsbook and prediction market loses money, and trying to claw back losses puts users in even deeper financial holes, experts warn. Unsurprisingly, those who lose the most are at the greatest risk of harmful mental health outcomes. Gambling as investment The Bank of America Institute survey found that Gen Z was twice as likely to see sports betting as a type of investment, versus 20% of respondents overall. For prediction markets alone, respondents overall saw them as a form of investing, but those numbers were again higher for Gen Z. In Betterment's retail investor survey, 52% of Gen Z respondents said they moved money originally meant for investment to sports betting, while another 26% saw wagering as a part of their long-term financial strategy. Management at sportsbooks DraftKings and FanDuel typically say their products are entertainment, not  investment. Prediction market platforms say event contracts, no matter the category, are a financial derivative. Dan Egan, director of behavioral finance and investing at Betterment, said sports betting increasingly appears alongside traditional investments on the same app or device, helping drive the association. The conflation is concerning because of the highly active behavior required to manage wagers on sports, unlike a long-term investment, Egan said. "It's not an asset that grows with the economy, that kind of gets better as time goes on, that has a positive expected return, and that you can kind of sit back and not have to do anything with," he said. "It's the exact opposite." Bank of America also found that the median deposit account balance for households use online betting was 59% of balances for those who didn't. An August survey by BadCredit found that 44% of survey respondents started trading on prediction market platforms in hopes of scoring extra income. That's despite the fact the majority of sportsbooks and prediction market users lose money. "People tend to tell other people how much money they've made," said Erica Sandberg, a consumer finance expert at BadCredit. "If you've got people around you who are saying, 'I just made $300 in five minutes on this platform,' you're gonna hear about it. You will not hear that they lost $800 last month." Woman student, fatigue with headache and university burnout, stress for paper deadline or study for exam in library. Campus, college and tired studying with scholarship problem and mental health pain Peopleimages | Istock | Getty Images Mental health worries How a sports betting addiction develops, and when it gets to the point where treatment is needed, varies by individual. But, there are common warning signs, Grant said. "It creeps into the way that they're functioning in the world, how they interact with their peers, how they interact with family," she said. "They lose time on work, they lose time in school. So when you start to see what we call clinically, 'functional impairment,' that things are interfering with the way that they're trying to navigate the world, that's when we really start to look at how this is developing into being a problem." It's little surprise young people are more likely to take up sports wagers as biological development brings a heightened appetite for risk, said Amaura Kemmerer at UWill, a mental health and wellness provider helping to support more than four million students at 500 institutions around the world. Consequences often arise well short of clinical treatment. Even players who are only dabbling, and "doing it occasionally … are still having predictable negative effects on academics," Kemmerer said, noting the impact sports betting is having on Gen Z college students. As a result, the perfect place to help combat the negative effects of gambling is on college campuses, both Kemmerer and Grant said, noting campus counseling services should treat it as they would other types of addiction. Betting platforms themselves have tried to mitigate risks. All regulated sportsbooks and prediction market exchanges have age verification tools. FanDuel and DraftKings let users set self-imposed deposit or time limits. FanDuel also imposes monthly deposit limits on accounts held by users under age 26. Polymarket on Wednesday announced optional self-imposed limits and a partnership with Birches Health to give users access to mental health resources. Kalshi does the same, as well as directing 18-to-21-year-old users to risk-management programs after they place their first trades. It donated $2 million in May to the National Council on Problem Gambling. "We've prioritized making Kalshi the safest venue for people to trade on," spokesperson Elisabeth Diana said in a statement. Experts stressed that not all forms of sports betting are harmful, but emphasized that motivation and frequency need to be clear, especially for young people. "Lots of people do it to make things more interesting," Egan said. "It makes the game more exciting. You just have to figure out how to say this is entertainment." If you or someone you know has a gambling addiction, call the National Council on Problem Gambling hotline: 1-800-522-4700. title: Voting in Brazil's 2026 presidential election has begun, with polls showing Lula and Bolsonaro nearly tied
body: Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Brazil Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff Dmytro Hubenko | Wesley Rahn with Reuters, AFP, AP Published 10/04/2026 Published October 4, 2026 last updated 10/05/2026 last updated October 5, 2026 Populist Flavio Bolsonaro has secured a thin lead over incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but the next president of Brazil will be decided in the runoff round, according to the country’s electoral court. https://p.dw.com/p/5NiO9 The early count in the Brazilian presidential election puts Flavio Bolsonaro (left) ahead of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva Image: Alexandre Meneghini/Pilar Olivares/REUTERS Advertisement With votes being counted in Brazil following the presidential election on Sunday, populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro was leading the race ahead of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro seeks to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro, while Lula is seeking his fourth non-consecutive term. Commenting on the outcome, Lula said they were "unexpected" as he was convinced he would "win in the first round." "We are in extra time," the 80-year-old said. "In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people." With more than 99% of the ballots processed, Flavio Bolsonaro has received 47.2% of the vote. Lula has 45%, according to the electoral court. Since neither candidate received enough votes to win outright on Sunday, the court announced that Bolsonaro and Lula will face each other in a runoff. Bolsonaro is monitoring the vote count in Brasilia, the country's capital, while Lula is following it from Sao Paulo. Because Brazil uses electronic voting machines, final results are expected to be available within several hours of the polls closing. You can watch our livestream on the Brazil election results below. Right gaining momentum in Brazil Fabio de Sa e Silva, a professor of Brazilian studies at the University of Oklahoma, told DW that the right was currently on the rise in Brazil, making it difficult for Lula to change the course of the election. "He still has a chance, based on the numbers, but the momentum is with the right," said de Sa e Silva. "The big news tomorrow will be not that we have a runoff... but it is a takeover that happened in Congress by the far-right," the researcher said. He added that it will be very hard for Lula to govern with Brazil's new Congress, even if he eventually secures another term. Lula vows to 'defeat the far right' Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo. Long queues of voters were seen in parts of Rio de Janeiro Image: Bruna Prado/AP Photo/picture alliance The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right ." Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city. Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution. "The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday. The 80-year-old Lula is seeking the presidency for a fourth and final time Image: Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS Bolsonaro calls for 'change' Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana. He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him. Flavio Bolsonaro has said he would pardon his father if elected Image: Douglas Shineidr/AFP The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent." "Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed." Brazil's 2022 election rematch The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected. Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump , who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial.  The US president called the case a "witch hunt." Brazilians vote in high-stakes presidential election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference." Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change. Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely." US President Trump had held close ties with fellow right-wing populist Jair Bolsonaro [FILE March 2019] Image: Chris Kleponis/CNP/MediaPunch/picture alliance What happens next? Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media. In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct. Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency. In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%. In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points. Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators. title: Bosnia-Herzegovina votes amid divisive campaigns, EU bid
body: Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Bosnia and Herzegovina Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election Jon Shelton | Dharvi Vaid Dhulia with AFP, AP, DPA and Reuters Published 10/04/2026 Published October 4, 2026 last updated 10/05/2026 last updated October 5, 2026 Bosnia-Herzegovina's three-member presidency is set to be dominated by nationalists from the three major ethnic groups, including Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, backed by disqualified Serb secessionist leader Milorad Dodik. https://p.dw.com/p/5Nim0 Preliminary results show strong results for ethnic-nationalist blocs Image: Armin Durgut/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Bosnian officials reported a record-low turnout following the Sunday vote, with only 41.5% out of the country's 3.4 million voters taking part in the general election in Bosnia-Herzegovina . Nationalist parties dominated races as citizens chose officials across multiple tiers of government; including members of the country's multiethnic, tripartite presidency. With counting nearly concluded, Serb nationalist Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, Bosniak moderate leftist Denis Becirovic and Croat nationalist ‌Darijana ​Filipovic have been announced as the winners of the presidential seats of their respective ethnicities. Cvijanovic had been backed by the Republika Srpska's former secessionist leader ​ Milorad Dodik , who was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process. "I am declaring that we have won," Dodik told supporters in Banja Luka on Sunday night. He said his SNSD party had retained the Serb seat in the presidency and remained power in Republika Srpska. Voters queued in Banja Luka and other cities around the country Image: Radivoje Pavicic/AP Photo/picture alliance With counting nearly over, Cvijanovic looked to have won with 55.6% of the vote. Social Democrat Becirovic won the race for the Bosniak seat with 38.1% of the vote, while Croat Filipovic took 48.2% of the vote. Nationalist and ethnic political division Voters also chose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and the Serb-run Republika Srpska (RS). Currently, about 50% of Bosnia and Herzegovina's citizens are Muslim Bosniaks, 31% are Orthodox Serb and another 15% are Catholic Croat. Between 1992 and 1995, more than two million people were displaced and nearly 100,000 killed in a civil war. Despite the country being peaceful for decades, ethnonationalist parties have kept divisions alive as a way to hold on to power. Many voters, however, say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric. The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges. There's been an economic downturn, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and sustained political gridlock — with dominant ethnic parties from these entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that binds them. The election saw contests that pitted the Bosniak ​SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party. Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results to be released later in the evening — though complex constitutional order and drawn out coalition talks mean that the true result of Sunday's election could remain unclear for months. What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina? The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the two semi-autonomous entities FBiH and RS, and the self-governing neutral Brcko district. These entities are further split into several cantons and communities. The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords , following the 1992-95 Bosnian war, itself a consequence of the breakup of Yugoslavia. Milorad Dodik still powerful figure in Republika Srpska In Republika Srpska , secessionist leader ​ Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remained the key figure of the election despite not being on the ballot. Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process. Dodik-backed Savo Minic decisively won the Republika Srpska's presidency and RS increased its heft by taking 39% of the parliamentary tally, up from 34.6% in 2022. After the vote, Dodik, who just returned from meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, thanked Putin and also credited "Donald Trump's magnificent victory" for keeping his political camp alive. He added that "now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners." Dodik, wants close ‌ties to Serbia and Russia and secession from Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday. What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina? In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state. The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism. Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union. Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO. Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022. But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption ​laws. title: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country
body: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country Image source, Social Media Image caption, The Flydubai plane was diverted to Saudi Arabia after passengers managed to take back control from the co-pilot By Claire Keenan Published 4 October 2026 Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel. The co-pilot is alleged to have attacked the captain with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers managed to overpower him and successfully take control of the plane. The Australian authorities have not identified the co-pilot, who has been named by multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times as Hamam al-Hammami. The prosecutor in the UAE has said it is investigating the incident and any possible motives. In a statement to the BBC, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed its investigation into "the man's links to Australia". The investigation involves state police and the country's security agency, it said, adding that an update would be "provided at the appropriate time". Sources familiar with the case, who have spoken to Australian media, have said the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014, and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, until he left the country. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) said the co-pilot's student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was no longer enrolled in a course, making him ineligible for it. Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he was an Omani national. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September was carrying more than 170 passengers to Israel. Two and a half hours into its journey, the plane plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) when the Omani co-pilot attacked the pilot with a crash axe , the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said. The pilot flying the plane, Capt Smit Machchhar, described how he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in. Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia. Figure caption, Watch: Flydubai pilot speaks with Indian PM Machchhar, an Indian national, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition. The co-pilot was arrested after the emergency landing and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu. The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said on Saturday investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident. He said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency. In the days since the attack more details have come to light about the co-pilot's employment history. While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline. It is also known that, from 2020, he was studying on a distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK. He graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.
