title: Debris found from plane that went missing off US coast
body: Rescuers suspend search for survivors after plane went missing off US coast - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat US & Canada Rescuers suspend search for survivors after plane went missing off US coast Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The search for the plane is being conducted near Nantucket, an island off the coast of the US state of Massachusetts By Sakshi Venkatraman and Toby Mann Published 3 October 2026 Updated 2 hours ago US authorities have suspended the search for six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston. The Coast Guard said on Sunday evening it was ending the search off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island, after 66 hours of looking for the passengers. "We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones," the Coast Guard said on Sunday. The Federal Aviation Administration told the BBC it had lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT). Authorities have notified the next of kin of those on the flight, four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals. Authorities had said earlier that they had located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft on Saturday evening. The plane departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT). According to the tail number released by the Coast Guard, the plane belonged to Latitude Air Ambulances, a company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home. Among those on board were two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News. The crew flew to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, who are not Canadian, Togeretz said. FlightAware's tracker shows the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft). Radio transmissions shows trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net. "You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?," the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?" The pilot's response was inaudible. "You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe. The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency. An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue". The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar". title: In Tigray, Ethiopian government forces have advanced against a northern rebel group, reports indicate
body: Ethiopia: Tigray airport reclaimed by government forces Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Conflicts Ethiopia Ethiopia government forces reclaim Tigray capital airport Wesley Rahn AFP, Reuters, AP 10/04/2026 October 4, 2026 Reports indicate Ethiopian government forces have made advances against a northern rebel group. Renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region. https://p.dw.com/p/5NiWS Rebel groups had seized control of airports and sections of Tigray's capital on September 23 Image: AFP Advertisement Government forces in Ethiopia said they have recaptured an airport in Tigray's capital that was seized by rebel groups last week, in the northern region's worst outbreak of violence since a bloody civil war ended in 2022. Several news agencies cited anonymous government sources on Saturday as saying Ethiopian federal forces now control Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle. "The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm," an Ethiopian general told the Associated Press on condition of anonymity. The AFP news agency, citing a "humanitarian source," reported rebel groups were leaving the city as Ethiopian government forces moved in. Neither side has issued an official statement on the status of who controls Mekelle, and reporting is complicated by communication blackouts and restricted media access. Return to civil war? Pulling out of Tigray's capital would be a setback for the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) , which recently aligned with several other armed opposition groups in northern Ethiopia. The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The TPLF has been the dominant force in Tigray since ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year, and then appointing former wartime regional leader Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president. The Addis Ababa-based government's Ethiopian National Defense Force has been fighting off a renewed rebel offensive since late September. The TPLF seized the airport in Mekelle on September 23, along with launching attacks on government positions in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, initially having made gains before being pushed back this week. Gebremichael issued a statement on Thursday, promising to continue guerrilla attacks on government forces, similar to what took place when rebels lost control of Mekelle in 2020. The TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, seeks to topple Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. More than 600,000 people were killed in a civil war from 2020 to 2022. Fears of wider regional unrest The renewed unrest in northern Ethiopia has led to tensions spilling across the region , with fears of wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa. For years, Ethiopia has accused its northern neighbor Eritrea of providing support to Tigray rebels, alongside Sudan and Egypt. All three countries deny this. Last week, Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties , with both countries expelling diplomats and closing embassies. The African Union said it was concerned by the growing tensions between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt, and has called on all sides to show maximum restraint. Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to the Red Sea The TPLF's Debretsion said in his video message that "the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea." title: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis
body: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis Figure caption, Major protest in Spain as millions struggle to find an affordable home By Ella Kipling Published 3 October 2026 Updated 4 October 2026 Tens of thousands of people have protested across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation. About 50 marches took place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona. "There is a lot of anger in the streets," a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union said. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city. The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase. Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property. Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer. His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament. Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87 Published 2 days ago Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit. Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Public broadcaster RTVE said nine police officers were injured and five people were arrested. Image source, EPA Image caption, Tens of thousands took to the streets of Madrid to protest Image source, EPA/Shuttershock Image caption, Tensions arose between some protesters and police officers in Valencia One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Union said there were 500,000, while officials put the figure at 70,000. Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city". Some had also camped in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days. One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction." Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros. Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid". Spanish police said they had arrested three members of a far-right group, some of whom had performed Nazi salutes, as they tried to reach demonstrators in the square. On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives". It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, An encampment has been set up for days by protesters at Puerta del Sol in Madrid Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Huge numbers of protesters rallied in Madrid The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two decrees. The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by  so-called "vulture funds". The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union. MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166. Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country. However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure. Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September. The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued. Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage Published 23 September Evicted Spanish pensioner can move back home, lawyer says Published 5 days ago The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction. House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE. The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents. It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively. title: Peru: Fire burning on road to Machu Picchu kills 1
body: Peru: Fire burning on road to Machu Picchu kills 1 Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Nature and Environment Peru Peru: Fire burning on road to Machu Picchu kills 1 Dharvi Vaid Dhulia with AFP and LUSA 10/04/2026 October 4, 2026 One person has died and two others have suffered burns in a fire near the main access route to the historic sanctuary of Machu Picchu. https://p.dw.com/p/5NiW0 The Incas built Machu Picchu in the 15th century Image: Laurent Davoust/Zoonar/picture alliance Advertisement A blaze was burning near the main access road to the ancient Inca citadel of Machu Picchu in Peru , leaving one person dead and two injured, officials said on Saturday. The fire began on Friday in the Sacred Valley of the Cusco region, which also includes the Ollantaytambo train station — the busiest for travelers visiting Machu Picchu. "We have one elderly person who died in the flames and two others with second-degree burns," Miguel Osco, head of the Cusco Regional Office for Disaster Management and Safety, told RPP radio. How did the fire start? Osco said the fire originated from controlled bush burning that farmers carry out to clear land for crops. The flames spread quickly because of the hot, windy weather and dry vegetation, he added. The Incas built Machu Picchu in the 15th century. Located at an altitude of 2,500 meters in the Andes Mountains, the historic sanctuary is regarded as an architectural masterpiece . UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1983. Machu Picchu is Peru's most famous tourist destination, attracting about three million visitors every year. title: Cornell president says university 'must do better' after frat house rape allegations
body: Cornell University president says school 'must do better' after rape allegations  - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat US & Canada Cornell president says university 'must do better' after frat house rape allegations Image source, Getty Images Image caption, A student has alleged she was drugged and gang-raped inside the Chi Phi frat house at Cornell University By Toby Mann and Ana Faguy Published 4 October 2026 Cornell University's president says the school "must do better" after a woman alleged she was drugged and raped by a group of men at a fraternity house. In an eight-minute video statement released on Saturday night, Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations raised by the woman, identified as Jane Doe, as "deeply disturbing". The alleged incident has raised questions around the culture on campus of drug and alcohol use, and the way investigations were conducted in the case, Kotlikoff said. Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the university when she says seven men from its Chi Phi fraternity assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine on 19 October 2024. She said she had reported the incident two weeks after it happened to Cornell University police, which investigated, but no charges were laid. Last month, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university, in which she alleged Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. Kotlikoff said Cornell was "committed to investigating" the way the case was handled, and said the school administration and community "must do better". "We must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent," he said. He added that university leaders need to create an environment where victims of sexual assault "feel safe coming forward and are treated with compassion and dignity". Kotlikoff said it is a "defining moment" in the university's history. "We must lead the way, we owe it to Jane Doe and to survivors of assault to get this right. And we must keep each other safe," he said. On the university's campus this week, the BBC saw growing frustration about the situation. Figure caption, Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case At a public hearing for students to speak about the alleged gang rape, many told the BBC they were ashamed of what happened and said the university had failed Jane Doe. "Our administration needs to change and it needs to change drastically and it needs to change fast," one student told the BBC. "Something like this never should have happened, this is a disgrace." As part of "broader work" that needs to happen, Kotlikoff said in his video statement that there should be a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life". "Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others, or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said. The university president also said that at the "appropriate time", the school would speak about how Cornell will "use this moment, this conversation, this anger, to help lead the broader effort to combat sexual assault not only on our campus, but beyond it". New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled, and has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead a review of the case. Kotlikoff said he supported the decision to appoint James to lead a criminal investigation, and welcomed an independent review by a law firm of how Cornell has handled the matter. Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent. title: AI giants 'not being nearly careful enough,' warns outgoing OpenAI safety engineer
body: AI giants not 'careful enough,' ex-OpenAI engineer warns Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Technology United States of America AI giants not 'careful enough,' ex-OpenAI engineer warns Nik Martin with AFP, Reuters 10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 Days after US President Donald Trump signed a voluntary pact with artificial intelligence giants, a former OpenAI worker said his industry needs the same safeguards as nuclear power or aviation. https://p.dw.com/p/5NiBc OpenAI has delayed plans for a public listing this year due to safety concerns Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement A safety engineer who recently quit ChatGPT creator OpenAI warned Saturday that artificial intelligence (AI) firms were "not being nearly careful enough." David Robinson's comments come amid growing concerns about AI becoming too powerful — a threat that US President Donald Trump has labeled a "hoax." OpenAI and Anthropic recently disclosed cases in which their AI models slipped past safety controls, hid mistakes and hacked systems they were not meant to access. How US, China could end the AI race To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did David Robinson write? In an op-ed for The Atlantic , Robinson said AI needs guardrails similar to those for nuclear power and aviation, adding, "The time for trial and error is over." He called for more emphasis on safety and research before US Big Tech develops more advanced AI models "so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster." Robinson, who oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier AI-model launches, said the recent errors were typical because tech giants are prioritizing "speed and flexibility." "An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to." The former OpenAI employee noted that the firm relies on "iterative deployment." It releases new AI models first and only tightens safeguards after problems show up. "As ​the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the ​level of care ‌that I believe is needed," Robinson, who worked at OpenAI for 3 1/2 years, added. Activists have staged protests calling on AI labs to slow development Image: Karl Mondon/AFP ChatGPT creator insists AI is safe OpenAI reacted to the latest criticism in a statement, "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage ​and secure, and ⁠we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down." In recent months, there have been repeated warnings from technology experts and policymakers that AI models are advancing so fast they could take control and possibly wipe out humanity . Despite those fears, US President Donald Trump is vehemently against stronger regulation, insisting that it will slow down innovation and make it harder for US AI models to beat Chinese rivals. This week, Trump announced a voluntary safety pact with six companies — Nvidia, SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alphabet's Google. The president described the deal as "morally binding,” even if it is not legally enforceable. He also directed his administration to rename AI as "Super Intelligence" or SI. A survey by Reuters/Ipsos last month found that three-quarters of Americans worry that AI giants are not doing enough to stop AI from causing serious harm to society. title: Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war
body: Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Conflicts Middle East Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war Kersten Knipp 10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing. https://p.dw.com/p/5Nhw3 Taliban security forces after a Pakistani airstrike in Khost, September 2026 Image: AFP Advertisement On Thursday night, Pakistan attacked targets in Afghanistan . The results of that attack are disputed. The Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist nationalist movement that controls Afghanistan, says that between nine and 10 civilians were killed, including women and children. But Pakistan claims the strike killed 22 militants and destroyed weapons and ammunition depots. These early October attacks are just the latest escalation in a conflict between the two countries that reignited mid-September, after months of comparative calm. The conflict was sparked again after a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces . On September 18, an attack on a police compound in the northwestern city of Kohat resulted in the d eaths of 31 people and more than 100 injured. A splinter group belonging to the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bordering Afghanistan. Pakistan accused Afghanistan of providing the TTP with a safe haven. Afghanistan denies this but clashes at the border and then airstrikes by Pakistan followed. Pakistani security officials inspect a mosque destroyed in an attack in the border town of Kohat, September 2026 Image: Hussain Ali/Anadolu/picture alliance TTP and Taliban: A complex relationship The TTP in Pakistan is not the same as Afghanistan's Taliban. Although it does have close ideological and personnel ties to the Afghan Taliban, it is an independent organization that fights the Pakistani state. Many of its fighters sided with the Taliban during that country's long-running insurgency against international and US troops. This is why, after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP gained more room and more leverage. This has meant that Afghanistan — a former ally of Pakistan — has increasingly become a threat to its neighbor. Pakistan has asked the Taliban to take action against the TTP, but the close connection between the two make this difficult. "Because of these personal connections and networks, it is extremely difficult for the Afghan Taliban to break away," says Conrad Schetter, director of the Bonn International Center for Conflict Studies, or BICC. How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The connections don't mean that the Taliban has any control over the TTP. There are certainly historical connections between the two, but Schetter doesn't believe that equals any sort of strong, direct influence. "The Taliban are simply not prepared to take orders from Islamabad," adds Thomas Ruttig, co-director of the Afghanistan Analysts Network, a think tank working between Kabul and Berlin. "They won't let anyone outside interfere." This means the Pakistani policy of supporting the Taliban in order to gain influence in Afghanistan hasn't worked. Difficult borders There's also another older conflict that has an impact on the current situation. This involves what is known as the Durand Line, drawn in 1893 by a British diplomat and an Afghan emir to mark spheres of influence between British India and Afghanistan. The current border between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows the Durand Line and also divides an area on both sides, homeland to Pashtuns, who make up the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan and second largest in Pakistan. So the border dispute here isn't just about territory, it's also about identity. "Ethnic and nationalist elements play a significant role in the conflict," Schetter tells DW. Many Pashtuns still refuse to accept the border that the Durand Line created. In Pakistan, the country's long-running rivalry with India also plays a part. A friendly Afghanistan would have been advantageous for Pakistan. But India has also strengthened its ties to the Taliban. "While Islamabad once viewed Afghanistan as a source of 'strategic depth' in its rivalry with India, it now increasingly views its north-western neighbor as a liability," an analysis by British think tank Chatham House notes. Pakistan exerts pressure Pakistan still has power over Afghanistan, though. As a landlocked country, Afghanistan relies on trade routes through neighboring countries, and Pakistan in particular. Pakistan can use border closures and trade restrictions to exert pressure even as the Taliban regime is trying to reduce dependence on Pakistan and find new economic and political partners. A Taliban soldier with an anti-aircraft gun on the border with Pakistan in April 2026 Image: AFP Trade and security considerations are now becoming tangled. Pakistan has held talks with the TTP that were mediated by the Taliban and ceasefires were agreed upon . Talks between Pakistan and Afghanistan also took place. But none of the temporary agreements resolved the crucial question of how to prevent attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory. So in parallel with diplomacy, Pakistan has also been relying on economic and political pressure, for example, by closing borders and restricting trade and by sending Afghan refugees back into Afghanistan. An analysis by the US-based Council on Foreign Relations notes that the Taliban are worried that if they crack down on the TTP too hard, they will drive the group towards another extremist militant group, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or IS-K. This group opposes the Taliban. The conflict recently escalated to another level. At the end of September, Kabul reported 28 killed and 32 captured fighters who had infiltrated Afghanistan from Nuristan province, Pakistan. The Taliban accused Pakistan of supporting its armed opponents, something Pakistan has denied. "It is known from past decades that Pakistan has regularly supported armed groups on the Afghan side — for example, the Mujahideen during the Soviet occupation and later the Taliban," Ruttig points out. "What's new though is that Pakistan apparently also supports parts of today's armed anti-Taliban opposition." Significant escalation This is turning the dispute over the TTP into a larger conflict in which both sides accuse each other of supporting armed groups from the other's territory. British think tank Chatham House speaks of a significant escalation compared to previous border skirmishes. Worryingly, a conflict over armed groups and border incidents is turning into a direct confrontation between the two nation states. Ruttig believes that it would be possible to contain the spiraling violence if both sides return to negotiations. "If both sides were willing to return to the negotiating table — perhaps with international mediation —there would be ways to contain the conflict and, above all, to protect the civilian population on both sides," he argues. Militants kill dozens of security officers in Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In a late September commentary in Pakistani weekly magazine The Friday Times , Pakistani analyst Saqib Ali Khan advocates for several things that could ease the tensions. That includes a reliable channel between Islamabad and Kabul, a separate approach for armed groups and greater involvement of the population along the border. The conflict, he argues, is not merely a dispute between two governments but also a security, border, economic and regional conflict. "Along those lines, there would have to be a shift in perspective on both sides," Schetter concludes. In the long term, greater economic integration is also needed, he adds, so that Pakistan and Afghanistan do not define their relationship solely through security and power issues. This story was originally published in German. title: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot
body: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Crime United Kingdom UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot Nik Martin with AFP, AP, dpa, Reuters 10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester. https://p.dw.com/p/5NhxA Police forces across the UK have stepped up patrols outside synagogues [FILE: October 2, 2025] Image: Andrew Matthews/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance Advertisement Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday. The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran , was foiled. What do we know about the case? Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam ‌A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, northern England. He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran. The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how ‌to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard. Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites. He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday. The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added. One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard. The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23. Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat. Heaton Park synagogue was the scene of a deadly attack in October 2025 [FILE: October 2, 2025] Image: Ian Hodgson/AP Photo/picture alliance Police find no link to RAF Fairford plot Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement. Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail. The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues . Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London. UK releases air base plot suspects To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives. UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed. Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran. The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran. Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents. Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023. Why has Brazil accused the US of election interference? Close In Brazil’s upcoming presidential election, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is facing right-wing challenger and ally of Donald Trump, Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Washington has backed closer ties with Brazil’s right wing, while Lula da Silva has accused Bolsonaro’s camp of encouraging foreign interference. The election has raised questions about US influence, trade tariffs, organised crime and Brazil’s sovereignty. The BBC's Ione Wells explains. title: Lula or Bolsonaro: Wall Street braces for two wildly different results in Brazil election
body:
Lula or Bolsonaro: Wall Street braces for two wildly different results in Brazil election Skip Navigation Markets Pre-Markets U.S. Markets Currencies Prediction Markets Cryptocurrency Futures & Commodities Bonds Funds & ETFs Business Economy Finance Health & Science Media Real Estate Energy Climate Transportation Investigations Industrials Retail Wealth Sports Life Small Business Investing Personal Finance Fintech Financial Advisors Options Action ETF Street Buffett Archive Earnings Trader Talk Tech Cybersecurity AI Enterprise Internet Media Mobile Social Media CNBC Disruptor 50 Tech Guide Politics & Policy White House Policy Defense Congress Expanding Opportunity Video Latest Video Full Episodes Livestream Live Audio Live TV Schedule CNBC Podcasts CEO Interviews CNBC Documentaries Digital Originals Watchlist Investing Club Trust Portfolio Analysis Trade Alerts Meeting Videos Homestretch Jim's Columns Education Subscribe PRO Pro News Josh Brown Mike Santoli Calls of the Day My Portfolio Livestream Full Episodes Stock Screener Market Forecast Options Investing Chart Investing Subscribe Livestream Menu Make It select USA INTL Livestream Search quotes, news & videos Livestream Watchlist SIGN IN Create free account Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Markets Lula or Bolsonaro: Wall Street braces for two wildly different results in Brazil election Published Sat, Oct 3 2026 9:12 AM EDT Michelle Caruso-Cabrera @MCaruso_Cabrera WATCH LIVE Key Points "The Brazil trade is: Does Lula win or does Bolsonaro win?" said one economist. As Bolsonaro has come from behind in the last few months, Brazilian stocks have moved higher along with his poll numbers. In this article EWZ Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT This combination of file pictures created on Sept. 29, 2026, shows Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva at the Planalto Palace in Brasilia on Sept. 16, 2026; and Brazil's right-wing Presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro at the Maracanazinho gymnasium in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on Aug. 22, 2026. Evaristo Sa | Mauro Pimentel | Afp | Getty Images With the first round of Brazil's presidential election taking place Sunday, Wall Street is gearing up with starkly different market predictions depending on the outcome of the neck-and-neck race. "The Brazil trade is: Does Lula win or does Bolsonaro win?" said Fernando Marengo, chief economist at Black Toro Global Investments. Those names should sound familiar. Lula is 80-year-old leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is running for a fourth term against 45-year-old right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. If neither candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, a runoff will take place Oct. 25. In short, if Bolsonaro wins, Wall Street expects a rally in the country's bonds, currency and stocks. As Bolsonaro has come from behind in the last few months, Brazilian stocks have moved higher along with his poll numbers. In a recent note to clients, JPMorgan noted that the MSCI Brazil "rose by 0.25% on average each day that Flavio gained in the polls." Kalshi markets now show Bolsonaro favored to win 60% to Lula's 39%. Prediction markets are prohibited in Brazil, so they may not reflect local sentiment. In a note to clients, Aurora Macro Strategies senior advisor Richard Lapper said, "the balance has shifted toward Flavio over the past month, but not nearly as far as the prediction markets are pricing." Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon Bovespa since Nov. 1, 2016 Bolsonaro is the favored candidate of the markets because he's promising more fiscal discipline, something many economists say Brazil desperately needs. Debt-to-GDP stands at 81.9%, up 10% since Lula took office. "We need a 3-3.5% fiscal adjustment to stabilize the public debt in relation to GDP," said Leonardo Porto, Brazil head economist for Citi. And it can't just come from one-offs like privatization of state assets, he said. "Brazil needs a permanent fiscal adjustment." That means cutting spending or raising taxes — either of which will be difficult. Roughly 90% of Brazil's budget is mandatory, some of it required by the constitution. At 32%, Brazil's tax burden is already the highest in Latin America, according to the OECD, and its prospects for growth are low. But there's a lot to be gained if Bolsonaro wins and manages to implement a "robust reform agenda," said JPMorgan. The firm looks to what happened under his father Jair when he was in power from 2016 to 2020. Bolsonaro Sr. managed to pass pension reform, which saved hundreds of billions of dollars. It imposed a minimum retirement age of 65 for men and 60 for women. Previously, men could retire at any age after working for 35 years, and women could retire at any age after working for 30 years. On average, the male retirement age was 56, and 53 for women. During that period of reform, JPMorgan said Brazil's 2-year yields fell almost to 4.7%, and the equity market gained 130%. If Brazil enters another period of reform, JPMorgan analysts say interest rates could decline to their neutral level, 6% in real terms, 10% in nominal terms, and "we would be thinking about the MSCI Brazil upside potential between 21% and 41%." They believe the forward P/E could move from a current level of 8.6 to as high as 13.3, last seen in 2020. The currency outcome is "bimodal," said JPMorgan, with USD/BRL moving to 5.50 if Lula wins and 4.90 if Bolsonaro wins. The entire lower house, and one third of the upper house are also being decided in this election. The composition of the legislature will be a key factor regarding the ability to achieve reforms. Black Toro's Marengo points out that other recent victories by pro-business candidates in Latin America have led to big upside moves in the countries' stocks, bonds and currencies. He notes Colombia's risk premium compression "was about 200 points, and it was one of the stock markets that rose the most — something similar to what happened in Peru." Marengo cautions some of the move is already priced in in Brazil. As with all emerging markets, a key risk is rising global interest rates, and for Latin America in particular, the El Niño weather phenomenon which could lead to crop damage for agricultural exporters. body:
Will Spain's housing crisis lead to a snap election? - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Will Spain's housing crisis lead to a snap election? Will Spain's housing crisis lead to a snap election? Close Thousands of people are continuing protests across Spain, after Congress rejected a series of measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis. Lawmakers voted on two decree-laws presented by government in response to nationwide protests that followed the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her home. Abascal was evicted after she was unable to pay a rent increase by the company that owns her flat. The case triggered a broader movement across the country demanding affordable rentals, which have soared in recent years. The BBC's Guy Hedgecoe is at one of the protests in Madrid and looks at whether the government's defeat will lead to an early general election, which is not due until next summer. title: Flydubai co-pilot attempted 'terrorist attack,' UAE says
body: Flydubai co-pilot attempted 'terrorist attack,' UAE says Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Crime United Arab Emirates Flydubai co-pilot attempted 'terrorist attack,' UAE says Wesley Dockery | Roshni Majumdar with AP, dpa, AFP Published 10/03/2026 Published October 3, 2026 last updated 10/03/2026 last updated October 3, 2026 The man, who stabbed his fellow pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai flight, was reportedly barred from flying in his native Oman over security concerns. https://p.dw.com/p/5NgVl A replacement Flydubai aircraft landed in Tel Aviv, carrying passengers from the flight on which a pilot stabbed another [Photo: September 30, 2026] Image: Gil Cohen-Magen/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement The co-pilot accused of stabbing his captain during Flydubai Flight 1073 was wielding a crash ax and attempted to carry out a "terrorist attack," UAE investigators said Saturday, according to Emirati state news agency WAM. A crash ax is typically stored in the plane's cockpit for use in case of an emergency. According to a Reuters media report based on unnamed sources familiar with the matter, the suspect is an Omani national. The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted radical ideological views. What happened on the Flydubai flight? The attack that took place on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has raised many questions about how the incident unfolded as well as about background checks in aviation hiring. There were 182 people on board, including four pilots. After the co-pilot stabbed the captain in an apparent attempt to crash the plane , two other pilots in the cabin took control and landed the aircraft safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Anwar Gargash, an Emirati presidential adviser, referred to the Flydubai incident on X, saying the latest "terrorist operation" showed the Mideast region's "fight against extremism continues." Flydubai co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman over security concerns The Wall Street Journal report said the co-pilot was hired by Flydubai despite the ban by Oman, allowing him to fly the jet on a sensitive route connecting the UAE and Israel. Israel and the UAE, which includes Dubai, signed the Abraham Accords normalizing relations in 2020. The newspaper said it could not be determined whether Oman shared concerns about the pilot's radicalization with other countries or airlines. The nature of his radicalization was also not clear. US broadcaster CNN cited two sources saying the co-pilot was removed from a job at Oman's national airline last year over concerns about extremist views. Saudi broadcaster Al Arabiya, also citing an informed source, reported that Omani authorities determined that the co-pilot held extremist views. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday in a video statement that they know the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination" and intended to crash the jet. Netanyahu also said they were also looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning that whoever was involved would pay a "heavy price." The investigation is ongoing. A Gulf diplomat, in comments to AP, said authorities were attempting to find out whether the Omani co-pilot was a "lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups." title: Morocco's first female head of government: Symbol or real reform?
body: Morocco's first female leader: Symbol or real reform? Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Morocco Morocco's first female leader: Symbol or real reform? Cathrin Schaer 10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 Fatima Zahra Mansouri has been chosen as Morocco's first female prime minister. Is her appointment a kind of symbolism, to show Morocco in a positive light? Or could Mansouri bring genuine changes for Moroccan women? https://p.dw.com/p/5NfFo Mansouri has been nicknamed the "pasha's daughter" because she comes from a prominent Marrakesh family and her father was formerly a pasha or municipal governor Image: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP Advertisement After the announcement that Morocco would appoint its first female head of government – Marrakech mayor Fatima Zahra Mansouri – citizens interviewed by local television reporters were mostly enthusiastic. "It would be great if we had a female prime minister for a change. She'd lift our spirits a bit," one woman said. "Why don't we give women a chance? We've never had one [a female head of government] before," said another. "May God bless her and help her stay on a straight path." "Regardless of who takes on the role, it should be a change for the better in Morocco," a man added. Morocco's King Mohammed VI chose Fatima Zahra Mansouri to be the country's first female prime minister following September's parliamentary elections Image: Mosa'ab Elshamy/AP Photo/picture alliance But there were also naysayers. Some locals questioned how she would take part in official events where tradition and protocol dictate that only men attend. "People are saying that a nation cannot succeed if a woman is in charge, even if she's only half in charge," one man told a television reporter, referring to the fact that Morocco's King Mohammed VI has the final say in national politics. Morocco is a constitutional monarchy, so elections are held but the king has ultimate executive power. The head of the country's government, or prime minister, leads the cabinet and administration and executes public policy. The king chose Fatima Zahra Mansouri, minister of planning and mayor of Marrakesh, over Fouzi Lekjaa, head of Morocco's football federation and budget minister. The pair are senior members of the Authenticity and Modernity Party, or PAM , which won the most seats in the country's parliamentary elections in September. "If you talk to Moroccans, there are some who are really proud of having a woman at the top and they see a chance for her to have impact on women's representation in society," confirms Anja Freudenreich, who heads the Morocco office of Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation (FES) in Rabat. "But others see her appointment as bare symbolism." Mansouri will lead what is colloquially being called the "World Cup government" as Morocco prepares to invest billions before it hosts the 2030 football World Cup along with Spain and Portugal. Mansouri is seen to have shown leadership after the devastating 2023 Morocco earthquake . Her appointment makes her the third woman to lead a government in the Arab world. Morrocan women have become more visible in local politics in recent years. Casablanca and Rabat both have female mayors, and there are a number of female cabinet ministers Image: Abu Adem Muhammed/Anadolu/picture alliance Will Mansouri improve the lot of Moroccan women? There is no doubt that Mansouri's appointment has important symbolic value, observers say. Two Tunisian women, Najla Bouden and current prime minister Sara Zaafarani, became heads of an Arab government before Mansouri's appointment. A 2022 survey by polling organization Arab Barometer found Tunisian attitudes towards women in power had changed as a result. Researchers from Arab Barometer believed the change — with only 40% agreeing that "in general, men are better at political leadership than women" in 2022 compared to 56% four years earlier — was the result of a "role-model effect." Before the appointment of Bouden and Zaafarani, there had been no major changes, they pointed out. According to a 2025 survey by the organization, attitudes toward women's roles have also been changing in Morocco. Mansouri could accelerate that. "We've already noticed how impactful this [appointment] is in terms of social and cultural norms," said Stephanie Willman Bordat, co-founder of Rabat-based advocacy organization, Mobilizing for Rights Associates (MRA). "People in public spaces, in cafes, on trains on their commute and just regular folks are having conversations about women's leadership and the taboo that says women can't be heads of government or women can't be bosses of men. There's good public debate and dialogue on this." "And on a global level, in terms of women's participation, this is really something to encouraging," Bordat, who has lived in Morocco for two decades, told DW. "Especially when you look at the global climate of backlash and regression in women's rights." Mansouri's prime ministership "is certainly notable as female leadership in the region is rare," Freudenreich of FES agreed. "It does have a highly symbolic character and I'm sure she does, or she will have, a role model function for women and girls in Morocco as well as in the region." No major changes from past However, Mansouri is unlikely to initiate a major change from past politics, Freudenreich suggested. She's more of a pragmatist than a rebel — a quality that's likely to see her navigate the much-discussed issues of protocol — and her party's electoral manifesto doesn't go into any major detail on women's issues, she pointed out. Before the September elections, MRA looked at which parties had women's issues in their electoral manifestos. Mansouri's party, PAM, appeared to offer only three such policies. PAM said it wanted to increase female economic activity, increase vulnerable widows' pensions and ensure better obstetric care. Image: Jalal Morchidi/Anadolu/picture alliance Other parties were more vocal on women's issues than PAM, with some saying they would push for updates to the Moroccan family code, or "moudawana." This sets rules on all-important aspects of Moroccan women's lives like custody of children, divorce, property rights , marriage, polygamy and domestic violence. It has not been updated since 2004. Did the king pick a symbol or is he genuine? In 2023, King Mohammed VI asked the then-prime minister to look into further updates to the family code. Discussions around that are ongoing and reforms are still pending, MRA's Bordat said. "But what's really interesting is that now we can say, well, women can be heads of government so women can also be heads or co-heads of family," she argued. The Moroccan king, who took the throne in 1999, has been broadly supportive of women's rights, Ahmed Benchemsi, advocacy and communications director for Human Rights Watch's Middle East and North Africa division, confirmed. Still, his organization would like to see things improve further. "With regard to women's rights, a symbol won't serve women's rights as much as legal reform," Benchemsi told DW. Morocco is generally considered comparatively progressive in women's rights and the 2011 Constitution guarantees equality between men and women Image: Moe Zoyari/Sipa USA/picture alliance "Activism around women's rights remains relatively permitted — an exception to the heightened governmental scrutiny and judicial proceedings against other areas of activism in Morocco," the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace wrote in a July 2025 commentary . "The king's leadership on gender reforms creates space for this activity, as advocates are often working in conjunction with parts of the government rather than against it." Given popular discontent with the economy and high youth unemployment and protests, "improving women's status is a promise the government can deliver on in a challenging period," the organization noted. But right now, Bordat argued that Mansouri's appointment shouldn't be seen as "something to be either celebrated or criticized." The country is still waiting to see how Mansouri will form a governing coalition, she argued. How many female ministers the new government appoints, and what powers they are granted, will also be closely observed. After that, "the real question is what civil society organizations, NGOs and citizens will do with this opportunity?" Bordat concluded. "That is, how do we hold all of the political parties and all of the newly elected representatives accountable and engaged … so we can continue to advance women's rights in Morocco?" Edited by: R. Casey Cathrin Schaer Author for the Middle East desk. title: Bosnia and Herzegovina is still shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions
body: Bosnia-Herzegovina shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Politics Bosnia and Herzegovina Bosnia-Herzegovina shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions Zoran Arbutina 10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 Bosnia and Herzegovina is governed by a system established after the Bosnian war — more than 30 years ago. Ethnic divisions, a complex administration and European integration all shape the country's political reality. https://p.dw.com/p/5Nfi1 Sarajevo, host of the 1984 Winter Olympics, was under siege for four years during the Bosnian war in the mid 1990s Image: Gabriele Thielmann/imageBROKER/picture alliance Advertisement To call Bosnia and Herzegovina a complicated country is an understatement. The country in the Balkan Peninsula divides its economic, administrative and political responsibilities between the multiethnic central government, the self-governing neutral Brcko district and two semi-autonomous entities that, for the most part, operate independently — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska . Both semi-autonomous entities are further split into several cantons and communities, home to mostly Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats in the central-western federation and Bosnian Serbs in Republika Srpska, to the north and east. This principle of ethnic nationalism is key to the country's central constitutional and political organization. The Bosnian constitution recognizes Bosniaks, who are predominantly Muslim, the largely Orthodox Bosnian Serbs and primarily Catholic Bosnian Croats as "constituent peoples" with equal rights. Today, the country has a population of around 3.1 million people. Around half are Bosniaks, while 31% are Serb and 15% are Croat. The rest of the inhabitants belong either to one of the 17 officially recognized minorities, like the Roma and Jews , or chose not to identify with any ethnicity at the last official census. Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian are all recognized as official languages. The central government is led by rotating three-way presidency , made up of one representative from each of the three main constituent groups. The upper house of parliament and key government offices are also divided according to this principle. This strict balance between the three groups is always maintained, both politically and socially, often leading to ethnic interests and political gridlock dominating the decision-making process. Dayton Peace Accords brought an end to war This complex, convoluted and oft dysfunctional structure was set up during the 1995 Dayton Peace Accords , and then anchored in the constitution. It was intended to bring an end to the Bosnian war — sparked by the breakup of Yugoslavia in the early 1990s — and legally secure the balance of power between the three feuding ethnic groups. During the war, from 1992 to 1995, the armed forces of the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats initially fought each other, before all three groups began to clash. Later, the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats joined forces to take on Republika Srpska. Throughout the war, neighboring Serbia and Croatia were actively involved in the fighting. Bosnia-Herzegovina: 30 years after Srebrenica massacre To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The fighting devastated wide swaths of the country, and resulted in countless war crimes — among them the nearly four-year siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica genocide , in which thousands of Bosniaks were killed at the hands of Serb forces. By the end of the war, some 100,000 people had been killed. A further 2.2 million were displaced by so-called "ethnic cleansing," forced from their homes by expulsions and violence to flee to other communities or abroad. The fighting only ended after the international community, especially the United States, stepped up its involvement, culminating in the peace deal agreed at a military base near Dayton, Ohio in November 1995. International oversight — essential, or no longer relevant? Although Bosnia and Herzegovina has been recognized on the international stage since the signing of the Dayton agreement, and is also represented at the United Nations, the country itself is still, in effect, only partially independent. The Office of the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, an international institution responsible for overseeing the civilian aspects of the Dayton agreement, has been in place since a UN Security Council resolution in 1995. The high representative — Christian Schmidt of Germany until this past June, and currently filled by acting head Louis J. Crishock of the US — has sweeping powers. He can dismiss elected officials, pass laws, establish new government agencies and overrule all the country's democratic institutions. The Dayton Peace Agreement 30 years on To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video This authority is often referred to as the Bonn Powers, as they were negotiated during a meeting of the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn, Germany in December 1997. From 2002 to 2011, the high representative also acted as the EU special representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina. In recent years, there's been much discussion over whether the office is still relevant. Supporters have said the high representative remains a necessary guarantor of the country's unity and functionality. But critics have pointed out the negative impact on Bosnia-Herzegovina's democratic culture, turning the country into a de facto protectorate that, to an extent, frees local politicians of responsibility for their actions. Separatist ambitions surface once more The sharpest criticism has come from the Republika Srpska and Milorad Dodik, its most influential leader . Dodik, in office as prime minister and president of the Serb entity until 2025, views the office and the international backing it provides for a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina as an obstacle to his separatist ambitions. With strong support from the Serbian capital, Belgrade, Moscow — and, increasingly, the Trump administration — Dodik has flirted with several different scenarios to split his Republika Srpska from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In his interpretation, and that of Republika Srpska's political elite, Bosnia-Herzegovina is highly centralized and unitary, which undermines the independence and sovereignty of the Bosnian Serbs. Milorad Dodik (right, seen here meeting with Vladimir Putin in April 2025), continues to foster a close relationship with Russia Image: press service of kremlin.ru A similar sentiment prevails among the political representatives of Bosnia's Croats. Although they aren't considering separation, they are trying to squeeze more independence from the central government in Sarajevo — not least with the creation of a third, Croatian, entity. The plan, incidentally, also has the support of the government in neighboring EU member Croatia . EU support aims to 'foster regional integration' A potential path out of the current economic and political paralysis is rapprochement with the European Union — the "European perspective," as it's called in Bosnia-Herzegovina, officially supported by all the relevant political actors. Bosnia-Herzegovina formally submitted its application for EU membership in 2016, and the European Council gave the green light for negotiations to begin in early 2024. But the actual start of membership talks hinges on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, notably in the areas of rule of law, fighting corruption, the prosecution of organized crime and the functionality of state institutions. EU enlargement: Who's slowing? Who's advancing? Who's next? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The EU has been financially supporting Bosnia-Herzegovina since 2007 in the framework of pre-accession assistance, and the country is also expected to benefit from the European Commission's Economic and Investment Plan for the Western Balkans. The plan aims to "foster regional integration" — and as a result, infrastructure funding for the Republika Srpska has been partially suspended due to its ongoing separatist rhetoric and policies. This article was originally written in German. title: Rising energy costs add to cost of living for Northern Ireland's consumers
body: Cost of living: Energy price hikes in Northern Ireland add to mounting financial pressure - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat N. Ireland N. Ireland Politics Rising energy costs add to cost of living for Northern Ireland's consumers Image source, BBC / Ryan McStay By Adam Mandeville and Clodagh Rice , Business correspondent, BBC News NI Published 3 October 2026 Households across Northern Ireland face increasing pressure on the cost of living as energy price hikes have come into effect. Northern Ireland's largest provider of natural gas, SSE Airtricity, increased its prices by almost 19% on Thursday for its 200,000 domestic and small business customers. That means the annual gas bill of a typical household in the greater Belfast and west gas network areas will increase by almost £172. The company said "unprecedented levels of volatility in global energy markets and higher wholesale gas prices" had led to the price rise. Wholesale gas prices in the UK have effectively doubled since the US and Israel began their attack on Iran. Keeping the house warm is particularly important for parents with young children and babies. Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave. She said she expects the winter months to be difficult because "most people are going to have to have the heating on, especially if you've young kids in the house". "There's no escaping it - everything feels more expensive and it is more expensive." Image caption, Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave She added that, despite "budgeting proactively" and "being as careful as you can with savings and credit cards", rising bills mean people's financial situations are out of their control. "You have to cut somewhere else and I already feel we are doing that," she said. Image caption, Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using her branch's free activities to combat the rising cost of living Lucy is one of the parents who attend a weekly baby class at Woodstock Library in east Belfast. Branch manager Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using their free activities to combat the rising cost of living. She said: "As well as families, we have lots of older people coming in now to keep warm." "We have people coming in who will stay all day, use the computer, have a chat and stay until closing time sometimes, so it is quite evident that we are providing an essential service at the minute when people are struggling," she added. Image source, Ryan McStay Image caption, Ryan McStay said he was "shocked" by the energy price increases Ryan McStay is a final year student at St Mary's University College Belfast, where he is studying to become a primary school teacher. He said he and his flatmates were "shocked" when they received a letter explaining their Firmus energy bills would be rising by 12.5%. "It shouldn't be normalised," he told BBC News NI. Ryan said increases like this exacerbate an already serious cost of living crisis for students like him. "The price of everything is rocketing. You're always second guessing and thinking about how much money have I got." The 21-year-old, who is from Newry, said the cost of living in Northern Ireland means he plans to move abroad after university. "I personally believe the best option for me right now would be to leave the country." 'It's getting worse' Image source, Naomi Campbell Image caption, Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie. She provides palliative nursing care to patients in their homes. "Many of them are affected by fuel poverty," Naomi said. "I think it is getting worse. People are struggling more, and the problem is that your energy needs increase hugely when you're dying at home. "Somebody is already struggling with the fact that they're dying. To then know that they can't keep their house warm." Naomi said a number of factors contribute to the increased energy needs, including the need to stay warm, different sleeping patterns, and essential medical devices. She said some patients have turned down services that could help improve their quality of life because they can't pay their electricity bills. Terminal illness adds further costs for patients, such as the cost of transport to and from hospital appointments, Naomi added. "I'm really saddened," she said. "The support is limited, there is very little out there. There is no reduction in costs of their electricity, even though their needs are so much higher and essential for their care." Naomi added that Marie Curie have called for the implementation of a "social tariff" for people with terminal illnesses, to ease their financial burden. "It would make such a huge difference to have that bit of extra money in your last months of life, so you're comfortable and you can spend it with your family," she said. She said some people spend the end of their life working because they "don't have any other access to money". "You end up dying not being able to keep your house warm. That to me is just devastating." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Households across Northern Ireland will get a one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from this month It comes as Share Energy announced electricity prices will also rise by 12.6% from today. This will add an extra £129 per year onto the typical household bill of their 41,000 customers. Head of Energy Policy at the Consumer Council Raymond Gormley said: "This increase has been driven by the continued volatility in wholesale energy costs, caused by geopolitics in the Middle East. "I suspect some of the other unregulated suppliers may follow suit and increase their tariffs." Gas prices outside the greater Belfast also rose on Thursday. Firmus energy has announced an 8.98% rise for 77,000 domestic and small business customers in the Ten Towns network area from 1 October. That means a typical annual gas bill will rise by around £87. It comes after an increase of 15.65% in July 2026. What support is available? Households across Northern Ireland will get the one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from this month. It will be applied automatically without the need for an application. The reduction is the local outworking of two schemes which apply in Great Britain, which has a separately regulated electricity market. The schemes are being funded by the UK government. Bank payment customers will have their bills automatically reduced while pay-as-you-go customers will receive £63 in credit when they top up their meter. The only complication for pay-as-you-go customers is they should not buy more than £112 of credit if they want to get the discount all in one go. That is because meters are set up to take a maximum payment of £175. Top ups over this value means the £63 payment will be split over a subsequent top up. Last month, applications opened for a separate means-tested scheme to provide a £100 voucher to some heating oil users. It is jointly funded by Stormont and the UK government. Two thirds of homes in Northern Ireland use home heating oil, the cost of which has also soared in recent months due to the US conflict with Iran. Data from the NI consumer council suggests 500 litres of home heating oil currently costs around £560, more than twice the price compared to this time last year. title: Australia: Car crashes into rugby fans, 10 injured
body: Australia: Car crashes into rugby fans, 10 injured Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus Israel Ethiopia German politics Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement Catastrophe Australia Australia: Car crashes into rugby fans, 10 injured Dharvi Vaid Dhulia with AFP, AP, Reuters and DPA 10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 The driver has been identified as an 18-year-old man who is said to have been "revving" when he lost control of his car. https://p.dw.com/p/5NgVn Police said the driver was arrested and taken to the hospital for mandatory testing [Representative image] Image: Hollie Adams/REUTERS Advertisement A car drove into a crowd of rugby league supporters in the eastern Australian city of Newcastle on Saturday after its driver appeared to lose control, leaving at least 10 people injured, authorities said. Several children were reported to be among the wounded. Two of the injured were in a critical condition, including a 5-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man, New South Wales officials said. What do we know about the car crash in Australia? The incident occurred in Newcastle's Wallsend ‌suburb, situated some 110 kilometers (68 miles) north of Sydney. Fans had gathered on the streets to cheer on the Newcastle Knights rugby team who were leaving for the National Rugby League grand final against the Sydney Roosters, slated to be held in ​Sydney on Sunday. Local reports cited the police as identifying the driver as an 18-year-old man, who was arrested and taken to the hospital for mandatory testing. Driver 'lost control' Newcastle Mayor Gavin Morris said in televised remarks that the driver was a rugby fan and that he lost control of his vehicle. "He was revving the car, he was excited, he was a supporter, he was there for the joy of the moment," Morris told Australian broadcaster ABC. "Somehow he lost control of the car ... and he's gone into the crowd." Police said they were probing the incident and initial inquiries indicated it was not terrorism-related. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the incident was "horrible." "Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans," he said in a statement on X.
